m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Install Visual Studio Code (VS Code), the editor you'll write every page in.
  • Add the Live Server extension so the browser reloads each time you save.
  • Get Chrome or Firefox up to date, since their DevTools are your X-ray glasses for pages.
  • Know the no-install fallback (CodePen) and the fixes for the setup problems beginners hit most.

Right-click on almost any web page and choose View page source. The wall of angle brackets you see is HTML: plain text that a browser turns into headings, pictures, and buttons. By the end of Module 2 you'll be writing that text yourself, and none of it costs money. You need three free things: an editor to type the files, a browser to show them, and a small helper that refreshes the browser for you.

Plan for about 20 minutes. If you're on a school computer that blocks installs, skip to the CodePen section and come back later.

#How the three tools work together

Tool Its job Cost
VS Code The editor where you write .html and .css files Free, from Microsoft
Live Server An add-on for VS Code that runs a tiny web server on your computer and reloads the page when you save Free
Chrome or Firefox Shows the page, and its DevTools let you inspect every element Free

You could double-click an .html file and it would open in your browser with an address starting file://. Two things go wrong with that. You have to press refresh after every change, and links that start with / point at the root of your hard drive instead of your project, so they break. Live Server gives your page a real http:// address, the same way a hosted website works.

#Step 1: Update Chrome or Firefox

You almost certainly have a browser already. This course shows Chrome and Firefox because both have excellent developer tools. Edge works like Chrome, since it's built on the same engine. Safari works too, but its menus differ from what you'll see in the lessons.

Make sure yours is current:

  • Chrome: click the three-dot menu at the top right, then Help › About Google Chrome. It checks for updates and asks you to relaunch.
  • Firefox: click the menu button (three lines), then Help › About Firefox.

#Step 2: Install VS Code

Always download VS Code from the official site, code.visualstudio.com (opens in a new tab). Search ads sometimes point to look-alike sites.

Windows

  1. Go to code.visualstudio.com (opens in a new tab) and click the Download for Windows button. This gives you the User Installer, which doesn't need an administrator password.
  2. Open VSCodeUserSetup-….exe from your Downloads folder and accept the license.
  3. On the Select Additional Tasks screen, leave Add to PATH ticked. If you see the two Add "Open with Code" action boxes, tick them too: they let you right-click any folder and open it straight in VS Code.
  4. Click Install, then Finish with Launch Visual Studio Code ticked.

macOS

  1. Go to code.visualstudio.com (opens in a new tab) and click the download button for macOS.
  2. Open the file from your Downloads folder. If it's a .zip, double-click it to unzip; if it's a .dmg, double-click it to open a window with the app inside.
  3. Drag Visual Studio Code into your Applications folder. Launch it from Applications, not from Downloads, so updates install properly.
  4. The first time, macOS warns that the app was downloaded from the internet and asks if you want to open it. Click Open.
  5. Optional: right-click (Control-click) its Dock icon and choose Options › Keep in Dock.

Chromebook

VS Code runs on a Chromebook through the built-in Linux environment.

  1. Select the time at the bottom right, then the Settings gear. Go to About ChromeOS › Developers, and next to Linux development environment select Set up. Accept the defaults. This can take 10 minutes or more, and a Terminal window opens when it's done.
  2. In that Terminal, type dpkg --print-architecture and press Enter. It prints amd64 (Intel or AMD chip) or arm64 (ARM chip).
  3. On code.visualstudio.com/download (opens in a new tab), download the .deb file: the x64 one for amd64, or ARM64 for arm64.
  4. Open the Files app, find the .deb in Downloads, double-click it, and choose Install.
  5. Open your app launcher. VS Code is in the Linux apps folder.

If Linux development environment is missing from Settings, your school has turned it off. Use CodePen (below) and ask your school's IT team whether Linux can be enabled.

Success looks like this: VS Code opens to a Welcome tab, with a narrow bar of icons down the left side (Explorer, Search, Source Control, Run and Debug, Extensions).

#Step 3: Add the Live Server extension

Extensions are add-ons that give VS Code new abilities. You need exactly one for now.

  1. Open the Extensions view: press Ctrl+Shift+X (Cmd+Shift+X on a Mac), or click the icon made of four squares in the bar down the left edge.
  2. Type Live Server in the search box.
  3. Pick the one published by Ritwick Dey. It has more than 80 million installs, so it's usually the first result.
  4. Click Install.

Nothing visible happens yet. In the next lesson you'll open a folder with an HTML file in it, and a Go Live button will appear in the status bar along the bottom right of VS Code.

📝 Note

You may also see Live Preview (by Microsoft) or Five Server in the search results. They do a similar job, but these lessons describe Live Server's buttons and menus, so stick with it for now.

#No installs allowed? Use CodePen

CodePen (opens in a new tab) is a free website where you type HTML and CSS into panels and see the result update as you type. It works on any computer with a browser, including locked-down school Chromebooks.

  • Go to codepen.io (opens in a new tab) and start a new Pen.
  • Type HTML in the HTML panel and CSS in the CSS panel. The result appears beside them.
  • Make a free account if you want to save your Pens.

The limit: a basic Pen is a single page. When a lesson builds a project from several files and folders, read along, try the parts you can in a Pen, and build the full version when you have a computer that allows installs.

#When setup goes wrong

⚠️ Watch out

There's no Go Live button. Live Server only shows it when you've opened a folder (File › Open Folder…) that contains an .html file. If you just installed the extension, open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, or Cmd+Shift+P on a Mac), run Developer: Reload Window, and look again.

The page opens in the wrong browser. Live Server uses your computer's default browser. Either change the default in your system settings, or in VS Code open Settings, search for live server custom browser, and choose Chrome or Firefox from the list.

The address shows a port other than 5500. Live Server normally uses port 5500. If another program is already using it, Live Server picks a different number. That's fine; the page works the same.

On a Chromebook, the browser can't reach the page. Pages served from the Linux environment are usually forwarded to Chrome automatically. If http://127.0.0.1:5500 doesn't load, try http://localhost:5500, and if that fails, http://penguin.linux.test:5500.

"Windows protected your PC" or a similar warning. Check that the file came from code.visualstudio.com. If it did, it's safe to continue. If you aren't allowed to install software at all, use CodePen.

#Further reading

  • Setting up Visual Studio Code (opens in a new tab): Microsoft's official install pages for every operating system, with fixes for rarer problems.
  • Live Server on the VS Code Marketplace (opens in a new tab): the extension's own page, listing every way to start and stop the server.
  • Installing basic software (opens in a new tab): MDN's overview of the editors, browsers, and local servers web developers use, and why each one matters.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Open a project folder in VS Code and create index.html.
  • Generate a page skeleton with Emmet and add your own heading and paragraph.
  • Start Live Server and prove that saving reloads the browser.
  • Open DevTools, find your heading in the Elements panel, and change it live.

Ten minutes from now you'll have a page running at an address like http://127.0.0.1:5500/index.html, and you'll have changed it in two different ways: once in your file, which lasts, and once inside the browser, which vanishes the moment you refresh. Knowing the difference between those two is half of web development.

#Step 1: Make a project folder and open it

Web projects are folders, not single files. A real site is a page plus its images, stylesheets, and other pages, and they all need to sit together.

  1. Create a folder for the whole course somewhere easy to find, such as Documents/web-course.
  2. Inside it, create a folder called first-page.
  3. In VS Code, choose File › Open Folder… and pick first-page.
  4. VS Code asks whether you trust the authors of the files in this folder. It's your own folder, so choose Yes, I trust the authors.

The Explorer on the left now shows FIRST-PAGE in capitals with nothing under it. Hover over that name and click the New File icon (a page with a plus sign). Type index.html and press Enter.

💡 Tip

Why index.html? When a browser asks a web server for a folder instead of a specific file, the server sends back the file named index.html inside it. Name your home page that way from day one and every server you ever use will find it.

#Step 2: Let Emmet type the skeleton

Every HTML page starts with the same dozen lines. You don't have to type them. In the empty index.html, type a single exclamation mark !. A suggestion box appears with Emmet Abbreviation in it. Press Enter (or Tab) and VS Code fills in a whole page skeleton.

Now change the title to My first page and type two lines between <body> and </body>:

You'll take this skeleton apart line by line in Module 2. For today, two lines matter. <h1> makes the main heading, and <p> makes a paragraph. Each has an opening tag and a closing tag with a slash, and the text between them is what shows up.

Save with Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac). Look at the file's tab: a white dot means unsaved changes, and it turns back into an × when the file is saved.

Here's what the browser will draw:

#Step 3: Go Live and prove it reloads

Click Go Live in the status bar at the bottom right of VS Code. (Or right-click index.html in the Explorer and choose Open with Live Server.) Your browser opens a tab with an address like this:

127.0.0.1 is a special address that always means "this computer". 5500 is the port, a numbered door that Live Server listens at. The status bar button now shows the port number instead of Go Live, and clicking it stops the server.

Now the proof. Put VS Code and the browser side by side. Change the heading text, press Ctrl+S, and watch the browser. It updates on its own within a second. That loop of edit, save, look is how you'll work for the rest of the course.

🧪 Try it yourself

Add a second paragraph under the first one: <p>My favorite food is ...</p>. Save and check the browser. Then delete the closing </p> from it, save again, and see whether anything looks different. (It probably won't. The next section explains why.)

#Step 4: Open DevTools and find your heading

Every desktop browser has developer tools built in. They show you what the browser actually built from your file, and they let you poke at it.

To do this Windows, Linux, ChromeOS macOS
Open DevTools F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I Cmd+Option+I
Open DevTools and pick an element on the page Ctrl+Shift+C Cmd+Option+C

The quickest way: right-click your heading on the page and choose Inspect. DevTools opens with the heading's line highlighted. In Chrome this panel is called Elements; in Firefox it's called Inspector. They work the same way.

Spend two minutes looking around:

  • The main area is a tree. Click the small triangles to open and close <head> and <body>. Elements inside other elements are indented under them.
  • Hover over any line in the tree and the matching part of the page lights up with colored boxes.
  • The Styles pane beside the tree shows the CSS rules affecting the selected element. You haven't written any CSS, yet your <h1> is big and bold. In Chrome those rules are labeled user agent stylesheet: the browser's own default styles.

#Step 5: Edit the page live, then refresh

In the Elements panel, double-click the text of your heading, type something new, and press Enter. The page changes instantly.

Now refresh the browser. Your edit is gone.

DevTools edits the browser's copy of the page in memory. It never touches index.html on your disk. That makes it a safe playground: try an idea in DevTools, and once you like it, make the same change in VS Code so it sticks.

🧪 Try it yourself

Select the <h1> in the tree. In the Styles pane, click inside the box labeled element.style { } at the top, type color: tomato; and press Enter. Watch the heading change color. Refresh, and it's back to black.

#The browser quietly fixes your mistakes

Here's a page that forgets to close any of its paragraphs:

It still shows three neat paragraphs. Right-click "Flour" in the result and choose Inspect: in the tree, every <p> has a matching </p>. The browser knows a paragraph can't contain another paragraph, so it closed each one for you.

This is the most important idea in this lesson. View page source (Ctrl+U, or Cmd+Option+U on a Mac) shows the text you wrote. The Elements panel shows the structure the browser built from that text. When a page looks wrong, the Elements panel tells you what the browser understood, and that's usually where the bug is hiding.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You change the heading in index.html, but the browser still shows the old text a minute later. What's the most likely cause?

  • Live Server reloads when the file is saved. Look for the white dot on the tab and press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S).

  • Once installed, it keeps working. Reinstalling won't help if the file was never saved.

  • A browser shows whatever the server sends; with Live Server that happens within a second of saving.

Show answer

A. Live Server reloads when the file is saved. Look for the white dot on the tab and press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S).

2You change a heading's text in the Elements panel, then refresh the page. What do you see?

  • DevTools never writes to your files. It edits the copy of the page held in the browser's memory.

  • Refreshing asks Live Server for the file again, and the file was never changed.

  • Nothing was deleted from the file, so the page loads normally.

Show answer

B. Refreshing asks Live Server for the file again, and the file was never changed.

3Your address bar says http://127.0.0.1:5500/index.html. Where is the page coming from?

  • 127.0.0.1 never leaves your machine; nobody else can visit this address and see your page.

  • 127.0.0.1 always means "this computer", and 5500 is the port Live Server listens on.

  • CodePen pages have a codepen.io address.

Show answer

B. 127.0.0.1 always means "this computer", and 5500 is the port Live Server listens on.

Key takeaways

  • Open a folder in VS Code, not a single file, and name the home page index.html.
  • Typing ! and pressing Enter makes Emmet write the page skeleton.
  • Save, then look: Live Server reloads the browser each time the file is saved.
  • DevTools' Elements (Chrome) or Inspector (Firefox) panel shows what the browser built. Edits there are temporary.

#Further reading

  • View and change the DOM (opens in a new tab): Chrome's own walkthrough of the Elements panel, with practice pages to click around in.
  • Page Inspector (opens in a new tab): the same tour for Firefox's Inspector.
  • Emmet in Visual Studio Code (opens in a new tab): more shortcuts like ! that save typing.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Lay out a project folder the way real websites are organized.
  • Name files so they work on every web server, not just your laptop.
  • Use Auto Save, Format Document, and comments to keep your code readable.
  • Follow a debugging routine, including the W3C validator, when a page misbehaves.
  • Know how the rest of this course is laid out.

A student builds a profile page. On their laptop the photo shows up perfectly. They upload the site, send the link to a friend, and the friend sees a broken-image icon. Nothing in the code changed. The bug is the file name: the picture is saved as Me.JPG, and the page asks for me.jpg. Windows and macOS shrug that off. The Linux computers that host most websites don't.

Habits like naming and organizing feel boring, and they prevent a surprising share of the bugs you'll meet in this course.

#One folder per project, with a predictable layout

Keep every project in its own folder inside your course folder. Inside a project, use the layout most websites use:

When you open a project in VS Code, open the project folder itself (profile), not the whole web-course folder. Live Server serves the folder you opened, so the home page ends up at a clean address like http://127.0.0.1:5500/index.html.

#Name files the way web servers like them

Four rules cover nearly every naming bug:

  1. Lowercase only. About.html and about.html are different files on most web servers. If everything is lowercase, you never have to remember which is which.
  2. No spaces. Use hyphens: my-trip.jpg, not my trip.jpg. Spaces turn into %20 in addresses and are easy to mistype.
  3. Keep the real extension. A photo is .jpg or .png, a page is .html. Don't rename a .png to .jpg and hope.
  4. Short and descriptive. red-panda.jpg tells you what's inside; IMG_20260914_112233.jpg doesn't.

⚠️ Watch out

Windows hides file extensions by default, so a file you think is index.html can really be index.html.txt, and the browser shows it as plain text. Turn extensions on: in File Explorer, open View › Show and tick File name extensions (on Windows 10 it's a checkbox on the View tab). On a Mac, open Finder › Settings › Advanced and tick Show all filename extensions. Creating files from VS Code's Explorer avoids the problem, because VS Code uses exactly the name you type.

#Save habits and tidy code

Turn on Auto Save. In VS Code, click File › Auto Save so it has a check mark. Your file saves a moment after you stop typing, and Live Server reloads the browser each time. If constant reloading bothers you, open Settings, search for auto save, and pick onFocusChange, which saves when you click away from the editor.

Format your code. Indentation shows which elements sit inside which. If your code gets messy, run Format Document: Shift+Alt+F on Windows, Shift+Option+F on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+I on Linux and Chromebooks. VS Code re-indents the whole file.

Leave notes with comments. Anything between <!-- and --> is ignored by the browser. Press Ctrl+/ (Cmd+/) to turn the current line into a comment or back.

Keep a backup. If your course folder lives in a synced folder like OneDrive, iCloud Drive, or Google Drive, you won't lose work when a laptop dies. Otherwise, zip the folder now and then and copy it somewhere safe.

#A debugging routine for when the page looks wrong

Predict before you look: what will this page show?

Every line came out as a giant bold heading. The <h1> was never closed, so the browser put everything after it inside the heading. Open the result in DevTools and you'll see the three paragraphs nested under <h1> in the tree. Adding </h1> after Shopping list fixes it.

You found that by looking at the tree. When you're stuck, work through these questions in order, because the early ones are the quickest to check:

  1. Is the file saved? Look for the white dot on the tab.
  2. Is the browser showing the file you're editing? Check the file name at the end of the address. It's easy to edit about.html while staring at index.html.
  3. Inspect it. Right-click the broken part, choose Inspect, and see where it sits in the tree. Wrong nesting means a missing or misplaced closing tag.
  4. Check the Console. In DevTools, the Console tab shows errors in red. A missing image appears there as a failed request with 404 (Not Found).
  5. Run the validator. Go to validator.w3.org (opens in a new tab), open the Validate by Direct Input tab, paste your whole file, and click Check. For the shopping list it reports, among other things, Unclosed element “h1”. with a line number. Fix the first error first; one mistake often causes several messages.
  6. Shrink the problem. Copy the file, delete half of it, and see whether the bug survives. Keep halving until only the guilty lines are left.

💡 Tip

When you ask someone for help, say three things: what you expected, what happened instead, and the smallest piece of code that shows the problem. A CodePen link with just those lines gets you an answer much faster than "my website is broken".

#How the rest of this course works

  • Module 1 (this one) is setup.
  • Modules 2 to 7 each have three lessons. Notes teach the ideas with live examples. A Build-along uses them to make one real page, step by step. Practice gives you new problems with hints and hidden solutions.
  • Module 8 is a capstone: your own multi-page website.

The examples in these lessons show code above a live Result frame. You can right-click inside any result and choose Inspect to explore it in DevTools. The frames can't see files on your computer, though, so whenever a lesson builds something, type it into your own project in VS Code. Typing it yourself, typos and all, is how the tags stick.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Your page uses <img src="images/dog.jpg">, and the file on disk is images/Dog.jpg. It works on your Mac. What happens on a typical web host?

  • That's true on most Windows and Mac setups, but most web servers run Linux, where Dog.jpg and dog.jpg are different files.

  • The server looks for exactly dog.jpg, finds only Dog.jpg, and returns 404. Lowercase file names avoid this.

  • Browsers repair some broken HTML, but they can't guess file names on a server.

Show answer

B. The server looks for exactly dog.jpg, finds only Dog.jpg, and returns 404. Lowercase file names avoid this.

2Every paragraph on your page suddenly appears huge and bold. Which tool shows you why most directly?

  • The tree shows what the browser built, so you can see that the heading swallowed everything after it.

  • The editor didn't cause this; something in the HTML did.

  • Saving more often doesn't change what the code says.

Show answer

A. The tree shows what the browser built, so you can see that the heading swallowed everything after it.

#Further reading

  • Dealing with files (opens in a new tab): MDN's guide to folder layout and file naming, with more detail on case and spaces.
  • W3C Markup Validation Service (opens in a new tab): bookmark it now. It catches unclosed tags and typos you'd otherwise hunt for by eye.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Describe the four stages a page goes through: request, response, parsing into the DOM, and rendering.
  • Read any element's parts: tags, attributes, content, and nesting.
  • Write a complete document skeleton and explain what each line is for.
  • Give a page an outline with headings, and add links and images with working paths and useful alt text.

When you press Enter on a web address, your browser sends a short message that says, roughly, "please send me /index.html". What comes back is not a picture of a page. It's text, exactly like the file you typed in Module 1, and the browser builds the page from that text in a fraction of a second.

Knowing how it does that explains a lot of things that look strange at first: why a missing image doesn't stop the rest of the page, why the Elements panel doesn't always match your file, and why the line breaks in your code vanish on screen.

#The browser asks, the server answers

A server is any computer program that hands out files when asked. On the real web it's a machine in a data center. In this course, Live Server plays that role on your own computer.

The browser never gets a whole website at once. It asks for the HTML first, reads it, and then sends a separate request for every image, stylesheet, and script the HTML mentions.

Each answer starts with a status code. 200 means "here it is". 404 means "no file by that name". Because every file is its own request, a 404 for one image leaves the rest of the page untouched; you just get a broken-image icon in one spot.

🧪 Try it yourself

Start Live Server on your first-page project, open DevTools, and click the Network tab. Refresh the page. You'll see a row for index.html with status 200 (plus a row Live Server adds for its auto-reload connection). Now add <img src="nothing.jpg" alt="test"> to the body, save, and watch a second row appear in red with status 404.

#Parsing: the text becomes a tree

The browser reads your HTML from top to bottom and turns each tag into an element, a little object in memory. Elements inside other elements become their children, so the result is a family tree called the DOM (Document Object Model).

This tree is exactly what the Elements panel shows you. It's built from your file, but it isn't your file: when the HTML has mistakes, the parser repairs them using fixed rules, and the tree shows the repaired version. That's why Module 1's unclosed paragraphs looked fine, and why the unclosed heading swallowed everything after it.

#Rendering: style, layout, paint

With the tree built, the browser works out how it should look:

  1. Style. It decides the CSS for every element, starting from its own built-in defaults (that's why <h1> is big and bold before you write any CSS) and then applying yours.
  2. Layout. It calculates the size and position of every element's box, given the window's width.
  3. Paint. It fills in the pixels.

Resize the window and layout and paint run again, which is why text re-wraps as you drag. You'll control the style step in Module 4.

#Anatomy of an element

  • <a ...> is the opening tag. a is the element's name (it stands for anchor, the original name for a link).
  • href="..." and title="..." are attributes: extra settings written as name="value" inside the opening tag.
  • MDN Web Docs is the content, the part you see.
  • </a> is the closing tag, with a slash.

A few elements, called void elements, can't have content, so they have no closing tag: <img>, <meta>, <link>, and <br> are the ones you'll meet first.

Elements nest like boxes inside boxes, so close them in the reverse order you opened them:

#The skeleton, line by line

  • <!DOCTYPE html> tells the browser to use modern standards. Without it, browsers switch to "quirks mode" and copy the bugs of browsers from the 1990s.
  • <html lang="en"> wraps the whole page and names its language, so screen readers pronounce words correctly and translation tools know what they're translating from.
  • <head> holds information about the page. None of it appears in the page itself.
  • <meta charset="UTF-8"> lets the page show any character: é, ñ, 中, curly quotes, emoji. Leave it out and an apostrophe can show up as â€™.
  • The viewport line tells phones to use their real screen width instead of pretending to be a desktop. Module 6 depends on it.
  • <title> is the text in the browser tab, in bookmarks, and in search results.
  • <body> holds everything visitors actually see.

#Headings and paragraphs give a page its outline

<h1> to <h6> are six levels of heading, like the chapters, sections, and subsections of a book. Use exactly one <h1> for what the whole page is about, <h2> for its main sections, and <h3> inside those. Choose the level by position in the outline, never for size. Size is CSS's job.

Many screen reader users move around a long page by jumping from heading to heading, and WebAIM's surveys of screen reader users keep finding that it's the most common way they look for information. A clean outline is how they skim.

Now predict: how many lines will this show?

The first paragraph shows as one line (or wraps wherever the window ends). HTML collapses whitespace: any run of spaces, tabs, and line breaks counts as a single space. To end a line on purpose inside a paragraph, as in a poem or an address, use <br>. To separate ideas, start a new <p>.

#Links: what goes in href

<a href="..."> makes a link. The value of href comes in a few flavors:

Kind Example Goes to
Absolute URL https://developer.mozilla.org Another website. Always include https://.
Relative path pages/favorites.html A file in your own project, found starting from the current file's folder.
Same-page link #where-they-sleep The element on this page with id="where-they-sleep".
Email mailto:club@example.com Opens the visitor's email app.

Relative paths trip up nearly everyone at first, so here's a project to practice on:

From this file To this file Write
index.html pages/favorites.html pages/favorites.html
index.html images/red-panda.jpg images/red-panda.jpg
pages/favorites.html index.html ../index.html
pages/favorites.html images/red-panda.jpg ../images/red-panda.jpg

A relative path starts in the folder of the file you're writing in. A folder name followed by / steps into that folder, and ../ steps up one level. Always use forward slashes, even on Windows.

#Images: src, alt, width, and height

  • src is the path or URL of the image file. (This lesson's frame can't see your computer's folders, so the first example uses a full URL. In your projects, use a relative path like images/red-panda.jpg.)
  • alt is the text that replaces the image when it can't be seen: for screen reader users, when the file is missing (look at the second example), or on a slow connection. Write what you'd say if you were describing the picture to a friend over the phone, and skip "image of", since screen readers already announce that it's an image.
  • If an image is pure decoration, write alt="" (empty, not missing) so screen readers skip it.
  • width and height in pixels let the browser reserve space before the file arrives, so the text below doesn't jump when it loads.

The red panda photo is by Mathias Appel (CC0), via Wikimedia Commons.

⚠️ Watch out

Paths from your hard drive. VS Code sometimes suggests paths like C:\Users\Sam\Desktop\cat.jpg or file:///Users/sam/cat.jpg. They work on your computer only, because nobody else has your Desktop. Keep the image inside your project folder and use a relative path with forward slashes: images/cat.jpg.

⚠️ Watch out

A missing quote swallows text. In <a href="about.html>About me</a>, the value never ends, so the browser treats About me</a> and everything up to the next " as part of the address. If a link or image suddenly takes half your page with it, look for an unclosed quote just before the damage.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A page's HTML uses two images and one stylesheet. How many requests does the browser make to load it?

  • Only the HTML arrives first. The browser finds the other files while reading it and asks for each separately.

  • You also need the request for the HTML file itself, which is how the browser learns about the other three.

  • One request for the page, then one for every file it mentions.

Show answer

C. One request for the page, then one for every file it mentions.

2Inside one <p>, your file has Hello, on one line and world! on the next. What does the browser show?

  • A line break in the source doesn't show up on screen; you'd need <br> or a second paragraph.

  • Whitespace collapses, so the line break becomes a single space.

  • It can. The browser simply treats the break as a space.

Show answer

B. Whitespace collapses, so the line break becomes a single space.

3You're writing pages/favorites.html. Which src shows the photo stored at images/red-panda.jpg in the project's top folder?

  • That looks for pages/images/red-panda.jpg, because relative paths start in the current file's folder.

  • ../ climbs from pages up to the project folder, then images/ steps into the right place.

  • That only works on one computer, and it uses backslashes, which aren't web paths.

Show answer

B. ../ climbs from pages up to the project folder, then images/ steps into the right place.

4A link's only content is a magnifying-glass icon, and clicking it opens the search page. What's the best alt for the icon?

  • That describes the picture, but a screen reader user needs to know what the link does.

  • When an image is the only content of a link, its alt text should say where the link goes or what it does.

  • Empty alt is for decoration. Here the link would be announced with no name at all.

Show answer

B. When an image is the only content of a link, its alt text should say where the link goes or what it does.

Key takeaways

  • The browser requests the HTML, then makes a separate request for every file it mentions. 200 means found; 404 means missing.
  • Parsing turns your text into the DOM, a tree the Elements panel shows. Rendering then styles, lays out, and paints it.
  • Every page needs the skeleton: doctype, <html lang>, a <head> with charset, viewport, and title, and a <body>.
  • Headings form the page's outline (one <h1>, then <h2> and <h3> in order). Whitespace in the code collapses to one space.
  • Relative paths start from the current file's folder; ../ goes up one level. Every meaningful image needs alt text that says what it shows or does.

#The finished files

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does favorites.html use ../images/red-panda.jpg while index.html uses images/red-panda.jpg?

  • It's the same file. Only the starting point of the path is different.

  • Relative paths start from the current file's folder. From pages/, ../ reaches profile/, where images/ lives.

  • ../ only changes which folder the browser looks in.

Show answer

B. Relative paths start from the current file's folder. From pages/, ../ reaches profile/, where images/ lives.

2Why are "Books" and "Games" <h3> instead of <h2>?

  • Size is never the reason to pick a level. CSS can make any heading any size.

  • Heading levels describe the outline. Subsections of an <h2> section get <h3>.

  • A page can have as many <h2>s as it has main sections.

Show answer

B. Heading levels describe the outline. Subsections of an <h2> section get <h3>.

3The panda on the favorites page has alt="". When is that the right choice?

  • Images that carry information need real alt text, or screen reader users miss it.

  • Empty alt tells screen readers to skip the image. Here the same photo was already described on the home page.

  • Then find out. Every image you publish is your responsibility to describe or mark as decoration.

Show answer

B. Empty alt tells screen readers to skip the image. Here the same photo was already described on the home page.

Key takeaways

  • Build the folders first (images/, pages/), with lowercase, hyphenated file names.
  • One <h1>, then <h2> for sections and <h3> for subsections, chosen by outline, not size.
  • href="#id" jumps within a page, a full https:// address leaves your site, and a relative path reaches your own files.
  • Inside a subfolder, paths to the top-level files start with ../.
  • Test every link, and use the Network panel to catch 404s.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Divide a page into landmarks: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, and <footer>.
  • Choose between <ul> and <ol>, and nest one list inside another.
  • Build a data table with a caption and proper header cells.
  • Write forms where every field has a <label>, the right input type, and sensible grouping and validation.

Picture two recipe pages that look identical on screen. One is built from meaningful elements. The other is built entirely from <div>, the "generic box" element. A sighted visitor can't tell them apart.

Now open both with a screen reader. Screen readers have a shortcut that lists a page's regions and another that jumps straight to the main content. On the first page those shortcuts work: "banner, navigation, main, content info". On the <div> page they find nothing, and the visitor has to listen to the menu, the logo, and the ads every time before reaching the recipe. Browsers' reader modes, search engines, and translation tools lean on the same structure.

Choosing elements by what content is, rather than how it looks, is called semantic HTML. This lesson covers the elements you'll use on almost every page.

#Landmarks name the big regions of a page

Element Use it for How many
<header> The introductory area: site name or logo, often with the main navigation Usually one for the page
<nav> A block of major navigation links One per menu
<main> The content that's unique to this page Exactly one
<article> A piece that would make sense on its own if shared elsewhere: a blog post, a recipe, a news story Any number
<section> A themed part of something bigger, almost always starting with a heading Any number
<aside> Related but secondary content: a tip, a sidebar, a "see also" box Any number
<footer> Closing information: credits, copyright, contact links Usually one for the page

The quickest test for <article> versus <section>: could you copy this chunk onto another site and have it still make sense? A recipe could; its "Ingredients" part could not.

<div> and <span> still have a job. They're meaningless wrappers you add when you need a hook for CSS and no semantic element fits. <div> wraps blocks; <span> wraps a few words inside a line.

#Lists: does the order matter?

  • <ul> (unordered list) when the order doesn't matter: a packing list, a set of features. Browsers show bullets.
  • <ol> (ordered list) when it does: steps in a recipe, a top-five ranking. Browsers show numbers, and they renumber automatically if you add a step in the middle.
  • Every item is an <li>, and only <li> elements can sit directly inside a list.

To nest a list, put the inner list inside an <li>:

Lists are also the standard way to mark up navigation: a <nav> containing a <ul> of links. A screen reader then announces that it's a list of three items before reading the links, so the visitor knows how long the menu is before going through it.

#Tables are for data with rows and columns

If information makes sense as a grid, where each cell is the meeting point of a row and a column, use a table:

  • <caption> is the table's title. Screen readers announce it when entering the table.
  • <tr> is a table row. Inside it, <th> is a header cell and <td> is a data cell.
  • scope="col" says "I'm the heading for this column"; scope="row" says the same for a row. When a screen reader user lands on "Library", they hear "Thursday, Room, Library" instead of a bare word.
  • <thead> and <tbody> separate the header rows from the data.

Before CSS could do layout, people built entire page designs out of invisible tables. Don't. A screen reader announces a layout table as data, row by row, and the result is nonsense.

#Forms that everyone can fill in

A form is a set of fields inside <form>. Here's a small sign-up form. Click the words "Saturday morning" in the result and watch the radio button select itself.

The pieces, and why each one matters:

  • <label for="email"> and <input id="email"> are a pair because for matches id exactly. Clicking the label focuses or ticks the field (a bigger target for fingers and shaky hands), and a screen reader reads the label aloud when the field gets focus, something like "Email, edit text, required". A field without a label is announced as little more than "edit text".
  • name is the field's key in the data the form sends. Fields without a name aren't sent at all.
  • type changes the field. type="email" checks for an @, and on phones it brings up a keyboard with @ on it.
  • <fieldset> and <legend> group related controls. For radio buttons, the legend is the question ("Which session?") and the labels are the answers.
  • Radio buttons with the same name form one group, so choosing one unchooses the others. value is what gets sent for the chosen one.
  • required makes the browser refuse to send the form until the field is filled in, with a message pointing at the empty field.
  • <button> inside a form submits it.

You can also wrap a control inside its label, with no for or id needed: <label><input type="checkbox" name="news"> Send me the newsletter</label>. Both styles are correct.

Field Markup What the visitor gets
Short text <input type="text"> A one-line box
Email <input type="email"> A check for a valid address, @ keyboard on phones
Password <input type="password"> Dots instead of letters
Number <input type="number" min="1" max="20"> Number keypad, values outside the range rejected
Phone <input type="tel"> Phone keypad (no format checking)
Date <input type="date"> A date picker
Pick several <input type="checkbox"> Each box on or off
Pick one <input type="radio"> One choice per name group
Pick from a list <select> with <option>s A drop-down menu
Longer text <textarea> A multi-line box

🧪 Try it yourself

The result frames in these lessons block forms from sending, so the button does nothing here. Copy the form into a page in your own project and open it with Live Server. Click Sign up with the name empty, and the browser stops you with a message. Fill everything in and click again: the page reloads, and the address bar ends with something like ?name=Jordan&email=j%40example.com&session=saturday. Those are your names and values. A real site would send them to a server instead of back to the same page.

#Mistakes that make forms hard to use

⚠️ Watch out

Using placeholder instead of a label. <input placeholder="Email"> looks tidy, but the hint vanishes the moment someone starts typing, so they can't check what the field wanted. Placeholder text is usually pale gray and hard to read, too. Always use a real <label>. Keep placeholder for a format example, like placeholder="name@example.com".

⚠️ Watch out

A for that doesn't match its id. <label for="e-mail"> with <input id="email"> silently links nothing. The quick test: click every label on your form. If the field doesn't light up, the pair is broken. A related bug: radio buttons with different names, which lets visitors select every option at once.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You're marking up the steps of a recipe: "Whisk the dry ingredients", "Add the milk", "Cook for 2 minutes". Which list?

  • Steps only work in sequence, and the numbers help a cook keep their place.

  • There's no default. Use <ul> only when the items could be shuffled without losing meaning.

  • That loses the information that these items belong together, and how many there are.

Show answer

A. Steps only work in sequence, and the numbers help a cook keep their place.

2A school news page shows five stories, each with its own headline and text. What should wrap each story?

  • A section is a part of something bigger. Each story makes sense on its own.

  • Each story could be copied to another site and still make sense, which is exactly what <article> is for.

  • The stories are the main content, not side notes.

Show answer

B. Each story could be copied to another site and still make sense, which is exactly what <article> is for.

3You click the label "Email" and the cursor doesn't jump to the email field. What's the most likely cause?

  • Labels work with every type of input.

  • The link only exists when the two values are identical, letter for letter.

  • Labels also give the field its spoken name for screen reader users.

Show answer

B. The link only exists when the two values are identical, letter for letter.

4Visitors can select all three of your "T-shirt size" radio buttons at once. What's wrong?

  • A fieldset groups them visually and for screen readers, but it doesn't make them exclusive.

  • Checkboxes allow several choices, which is the problem you're trying to fix.

  • Radio buttons only act as one group when they share the same name.

Show answer

C. Radio buttons only act as one group when they share the same name.

Key takeaways

  • Pick elements for what content is: landmarks for regions, <article> for self-contained pieces, <section> for themed parts, and <div>/<span> only as styling hooks.
  • <ol> when order matters, <ul> when it doesn't. Only <li> goes directly inside a list, and nested lists go inside an <li>.
  • Tables are for data grids, with a <caption> and <th scope> header cells, never for layout.
  • Every form field needs a <label> whose for matches its id, plus a name. Use the right type, group radio buttons with a shared name and a <fieldset>/<legend>, and add required where it applies.

#Further reading

  • Structuring documents (opens in a new tab): MDN's guide to landmarks and page structure, with a complete example page to study.
  • Your first form (opens in a new tab): build a contact form step by step, including what happens when it's sent.
  • Labeling controls (opens in a new tab): the W3C's accessibility tutorial on labels, including the wrapping style and when to hide a label visually.

What you'll learn

  • Lay out a whole page with <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, and <footer>.

Recipe sites are a perfect semantic HTML workout: they have a site header, a menu, a main article, grouped lists, numbered steps, a little data table, and side tips. Here's the page you'll build, still with no CSS of your own:

Scroll inside the result to see all of it, and click the three menu links: each one jumps to its section.

#Step 1: Set up the project

Make a new project folder:

Download the photo from its Wikimedia Commons page (opens in a new tab), save it into images/, and rename it pancakes.jpg. Open the recipe folder in VS Code, create index.html, type ! and press Enter, and set the title to Fluffy blueberry pancakes | Weekend Kitchen. Then click Go Live.

#Step 2: Sketch the landmarks first

Before writing any content, lay out the regions inside <body>. Comments mark where everything will go:

The recipe is an <article> because it would make sense on its own, say, shared to another cooking site. The <header> and <footer> belong to the whole site, so they sit outside <main>. On a real site they'd repeat on every page, while <main> changes.

#Step 3: The header and its navigation

The site name is a <p>, not a heading. The page's <h1> should name what this page is about, the pancakes, and the site name is the same on every page.

The menu is a <ul> of links inside <nav>. The order of a menu doesn't change its meaning, so it's unordered. Right now it shows as a bulleted list; in Module 5 you'll turn lists like this into a row of links with CSS. The links point at ids you'll add in Steps 6 to 8, so they won't jump anywhere until then.

#Step 4: Title, introduction, and a captioned photo

Inside <article>:

<figure> groups an image (or a chart, or a code sample) with its caption, and <figcaption> is that caption. Screen readers connect the two.

The caption also does a legal job. This photo's license, CC BY 2.0, lets anyone use it for free as long as they credit the photographer. Whenever you use someone else's image, check its license and give the credit it asks for.

#Step 5: An at-a-glance table

Prep time, cook time, and yield are a tiny grid of data, with headings and values, so they belong in a table. Add this after the figure:

Without CSS the table has no borders, and that's fine. The header cells are bold and centered by default, and the structure is all there for when you style it in Module 4.

#Step 6: Ingredients as grouped lists

Each group gets an <h3> heading and its own <ul>, because within a group you can gather things in any order. The whole block is a <section>: a themed part of the article that starts with a heading. Its id="ingredients" is what the menu link jumps to.

The fractions ½ and ¼ are real characters, typed or pasted straight in. They display correctly because the skeleton has <meta charset="UTF-8">.

#Step 7: The method as a numbered list

Steps only work in order, so this is an <ol>. Add it after the ingredients section:

You never type the numbers. If you add a step in the middle later, every step after it renumbers itself.

<strong> marks the one instruction people most often get wrong (over-mixing makes tough pancakes). That's importance, so <strong> is the right element rather than just "bold".

#Step 8: Tips and the footer

The tip is useful but not part of the main instructions, which makes it an <aside>. Put it at the end of the article, then fill in the footer:

Save, and click each menu link in your browser. All three should jump now.

#Step 9: Check the structure the way assistive tech sees it

Browsers build an accessibility tree alongside the DOM: a simpler version listing each element's role and name, which is what screen readers read.

  • Chrome: in the Elements panel, select <main>, then open the Accessibility tab in the side pane (next to Styles and Computed; it may be behind the » button). Under Computed Properties you'll see its role is main. Select <nav> and you'll see navigation.
  • Firefox: right-click the page and choose Inspect Accessibility Properties to open the Accessibility panel, which lists every element's role.

Then paste the file into the W3C validator (opens in a new tab). It catches a missing </li> or a <li> placed outside a list.

#The finished file

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why is the site name "Weekend Kitchen" a <p> instead of the <h1>?

  • They are allowed. The reason is about what the page is about.

  • The site name repeats on every page, while each page's <h1> says what makes that page different.

  • Size is never the reason. CSS can make a <p> as large as you like.

Show answer

B. The site name repeats on every page, while each page's <h1> says what makes that page different.

2Why are the ingredients in <ul>s but the method in an <ol>?

  • <ol> says "the order matters", and the numbers help a cook keep their place.

  • You can use as many ordered lists as you need.

  • The choice is about meaning. CSS can change or remove the bullets and numbers.

Show answer

A. <ol> says "the order matters", and the numbers help a cook keep their place.

3Why does the tip go in an <aside> rather than another <section>?

  • Without CSS, an aside appears in the normal flow like everything else. The element describes meaning, not position.

  • <aside> marks content that's connected to its surroundings but could be skipped without losing the main point.

  • There's no limit on sections.

Show answer

B. <aside> marks content that's connected to its surroundings but could be skipped without losing the main point.

Key takeaways

  • Sketch the landmarks first: site <header> and <footer> outside <main>, the page's real content inside it.
  • A self-contained piece like a recipe is an <article>. Its themed parts are <section>s that start with headings.
  • Menus are lists of links inside <nav>, and href="#id" links can target sections.
  • <figure> and <figcaption> keep an image and its caption together, and the caption is a good home for a license credit.
  • Use a table only for data in rows and columns, <ul> when order doesn't matter, and <ol> when it does.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a "Rate this recipe" form at the end of the article: a <fieldset> with the legend "How were they?" and five radio buttons sharing name="rating", each with its own label.
  • Add a nutrition table with nutrient names as row headers (<th scope="row">) and amounts per pancake as data.
  • Make a second recipe page, add a "Recipes" link to the menu on both pages, and link them to each other.

#Further reading

  • Lists (opens in a new tab): MDN on ordered, unordered, and description lists, including nesting and a recipe-style example.
  • Semantic HTML (opens in a new tab): web.dev's chapter on why element choice matters, with a before-and-after rewrite of a <div>-only page.
  • HTML table basics (opens in a new tab): how tables are built row by row, with spanning cells for when your data gets more complicated.

What you'll learn

  • Turn a page made of <div>s into one made of landmarks.
  • Pick the right list type, and nest lists correctly.
  • Build a table with a caption, column headers, and row headers.
  • Find and fix the label, name, and grouping bugs that make forms hard to use.
  • Build a complete registration form with the right input types and validation.

Make a practice-m3 folder and do each exercise in its own file with Live Server running. For the form exercises, that matters: the result frames on this page block form sending, but your own pages don't, so you can see required and the input types do their work.

#Warm-up: name that element

For each piece of content, which element fits best? Answer before opening the solution.

  1. The copyright line at the bottom of every page
  2. Five links to the site's main pages
  3. A blog post shown on the home page that could be shared on its own
  4. A "Did you know?" box next to an article
  5. A wrapper you need only so CSS can add a background color
Show solution
  1. <footer> 2. <nav> with a <ul> inside 3. <article> 4. <aside> 5. <div>: no semantic element fits, so use the generic one.

#Exercise 1: Rewrite the div soup

This page uses <div> for everything. Rewrite it with landmark and sectioning elements, without changing the text. Keep a <div> only if nothing else fits.

Need a hint?

Work from the outside in: the top strip, the menu, the main area, the one self-contained post, the bottom strip. Then fix the insides: the post's title should be a heading, the menu's links a list, and the text a paragraph.

Show solution

No <div> survived: every region had a meaningful element. The post title became the page's <h1> because the post is what this page is about. (Don't click the menu links in the frame; those pages don't exist here.)

#Exercise 2: Choose and nest lists

Mark up both lists:

  • My top three movies, best first: Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, Coco, WALL-E.
  • Beach day bag: sunscreen, water bottle, and snacks. Under snacks, list grapes, crackers, and granola bars.

Sample result: the movies numbered 1 to 3, the beach list bulleted, and the three snacks indented under "Snacks".

Need a hint?

A ranking has an order; a bag doesn't. For the snacks, the inner list goes inside the "Snacks" <li>, before its closing tag.

Show solution

<cite> marks the title of a creative work, and browsers italicize it. Plain text in the <li>s would also be correct.

#Exercise 3: A schedule table with row headers

Build this as a table, with the caption "Art club rotation", the days as column headers, and the weeks as row headers:

Need a hint?

The top-left cell has no heading of its own; use an empty <td></td> there. Each body row starts with a <th scope="row"> for the week, then <td>s for the activities.

Show solution

Now a screen reader user who moves to "Clay" in the second row can hear which week and which day it belongs to, not just the word "Clay".

#Exercise 4: Fix the broken form

Try clicking each label in this form. Some do nothing, and the radio buttons misbehave. Find five bugs.

Need a hint?

Check each field for four things: does it have a <label>, does for match id, does it have a name, and is its type the most specific one? Then look at how the radio buttons are named and grouped.

Show solution
  1. "Username" is plain text, not a <label>, so the field has no name for screen readers and clicking the word does nothing.
  2. The email label says for="mail" but the input's id is email.
  3. The email field is type="text"; type="email" gives the @ keyboard and checks the address.
  4. The password uses placeholder instead of a label, and it has no name, so it would never be sent.
  5. Every radio button has a different name, so all three can be selected. They also need a <fieldset> and <legend> so "Grade" is announced as the question, plus a value each.

Click the labels again: every one now focuses or selects its control, and only one grade can be chosen.

#Exercise 5: Pick the input types

You're building a form for a summer coding camp. Choose the best element and type for each field, and say what it gives the visitor.

  1. Parent's phone number
  2. Camper's date of birth
  3. Number of T-shirts (1 to 3)
  4. Camper's personal website, if any
  5. Allergies or medical notes
  6. Which week: June, July, or August (exactly one)
Need a hint?

Think about what keyboard or picker would appear on a phone, and whether the visitor picks one option, several, or types freely.

Show solution
Field Markup Why
Phone <input type="tel"> Phone keypad on mobile; phone formats vary, so no checking
Date of birth <input type="date"> A date picker, and no confusion about day/month order
T-shirts <input type="number" min="1" max="3"> Number keypad, and 0 or 4 are rejected
Website <input type="url"> Checks for a full address like https://…
Medical notes <textarea> Room for several lines
Week Three <input type="radio" name="week"> in a <fieldset> Exactly one choice, with the legend as the question

#Exercise 6: An event registration form

Build a registration form for a community "Code and Pizza Night". It needs:

  • Full name and email, both required.
  • Age, a number from 10 to 18, required.
  • A choice of one workshop: "Build a web page", "Make a game", or "Program a robot".
  • A T-shirt size drop-down: S, M, L, XL.
  • A text area for dietary needs.
  • A required checkbox: "A parent or guardian knows I'm attending".
  • A submit button.
Need a hint?

Copy the label-and-input pattern from the Notes for each field. A drop-down is <select> with an <option> for each size, and it takes a <label> just like an input. Test it in Live Server: submitting with blanks should be blocked, and a full submission should put every name in the address bar.

Show solution

Putting required on one radio button makes the whole group required: the visitor has to pick one of the three. The <br> before the text area puts the box on its own line until you learn CSS for layout.

#Challenge: A full community event page

Combine the module into one page for Code and Pizza Night:

  • A <main> with an <article> describing the event (what, when, where), including a <figure> with a captioned image whose license you've checked.
  • A schedule <table> (6:00 Doors open, 6:15 Workshops, 7:30 Pizza and demos, 8:15 Wrap-up) with a caption and header cells.
  • Your Exercise 6 form in its own <section> with an id the menu can link to.
  • A <footer> with the organizer's contact link.

Check it three ways: the validator reports no errors; Chrome's Accessibility tab (or Firefox's Accessibility panel) shows the right roles for your landmarks; and every label in the form, when clicked, focuses its field.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write a CSS rule and connect a stylesheet to a page.
  • Target elements with type, class, ID, descendant, grouped, and pseudo-class selectors.
  • Predict which rule wins a conflict using importance, specificity, and source order, and know which properties inherit.
  • Name the four layers of the box model and calculate how wide a box really is, with and without border-box.

Three rules below all set the color of the same paragraph, and the blue rule comes last. Cover the result with your hand and predict the color before you look.

It's crimson. "The last rule wins" is only the tie-breaker, and most beginners' CSS frustrations come from not knowing what happens before the tie-break. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to explain that result, and you'll know how to write CSS that doesn't surprise you.

#The anatomy of a CSS rule

  • p is the selector: which elements this rule applies to.
  • Between the braces are declarations, each a property (color), a colon, a value (royalblue), and a semicolon.

CSS can live in three places:

  1. An external stylesheet, a .css file connected in the <head> with <link rel="stylesheet" href="css/styles.css">. Use this in your projects: one file can style every page of a site.
  2. A <style> element inside the HTML. The live examples in these lessons use it so the code and its result fit in one block.
  3. A style attribute on one element, like <p style="color: red">. Avoid it. It can't be reused, and as you'll see, it beats almost every other rule.

#Selectors point at elements

Selector Example Selects
Type p Every <p>
Class .price Every element with class="price"
ID #signup The one element with id="signup"
Descendant nav a Every <a> anywhere inside a <nav>
Child ul > li <li>s directly inside a <ul>, not deeper
Group h1, h2 Every <h1> and every <h2>
Pseudo-class a:hover A link while the pointer is over it
Universal * Every element

Hover over the menu links in this result:

A few things to notice. In the HTML, a class is written without the dot (class="price"); in CSS, the dot means "class". An element can have several classes separated by spaces, like class="card featured", and each one can be targeted. And the sold-out price is still green even though its paragraph is gray. That's the cascade at work, and it's coming up next.

Classes are your everyday tool. IDs must be unique on a page and are best kept for jump links and pairing labels with inputs. You'll see below why styling with them causes trouble.

#The cascade: how the browser picks a winner

The cascade only matters when two declarations try to set the same property on the same element. Then the browser settles it by asking three questions, in this order:

  1. Importance. A declaration ending in !important beats normal ones. Treat it as an emergency tool you almost never use. (Even before this question, your CSS beats the browser's built-in defaults, which is why your rules can restyle an <h1> at all.)
  2. Specificity. The more precisely a selector targets an element, the stronger it is. Details in the next section.
  3. Source order. If everything else ties, the declaration that appears later in the CSS wins.

Inheritance is a separate idea that people often mix up with the cascade. Some properties, mostly about text (color, font-family, font-size, line-height, text-align), pass down from a parent to everything inside it. Box properties (border, padding, margin, background, width) don't.

An inherited value is the weakest thing in CSS: any rule that targets the element directly beats it. The browser's default stylesheet has a rule that colors a elements blue, so the link ignores the color it would inherit. Same story for the sold-out price above: .price targets the <span> directly, so it beats the gray coming down from the paragraph. To make links follow their parent's color, target them: .card a { color: inherit; }.

#Specificity is a three-column score

Score every selector by counting three kinds of thing:

  1. IDs (#intro)
  2. Classes, pseudo-classes, and attribute selectors (.note, :hover, [type="email"])
  3. Element types (p, nav)

Write the counts as three numbers and compare them left to right, like comparing words alphabetically. The first column that differs decides; the rest don't matter.

Selector IDs Classes Types Score
* 0 0 0 0-0-0
p 0 0 1 0-0-1
nav a 0 0 2 0-0-2
.note 0 1 0 0-1-0
p.note 0 1 1 0-1-1
nav a:hover 0 1 2 0-1-2
.card .price 0 2 0 0-2-0
#intro 1 0 0 1-0-0

Back to the opening puzzle: #intro scores 1-0-0, .note 0-1-0, and p 0-0-1. The ID wins in the first column, so the paragraph is crimson, and the order of the rules never came into it.

Columns never carry over. A selector with one class (0-1-0) beats one with eleven type selectors (0-0-11), the same way "b" comes after "azzzz" in the dictionary. Above all three columns sit inline style attributes, and above those, !important.

That's why experienced developers style almost entirely with single classes. When every selector scores about 0-1-0, conflicts are settled by source order, which you can see by reading the file. Use an ID, and the only way to override it is another ID or !important, and then the next fix needs something even stronger.

#Every element is a box

The browser draws every element as a rectangle with four layers, from the inside out:

  • Content is where text and images go. width and height set its size.
  • Padding is space between the content and the border. The element's background fills it, so it's what gives a button breathing room around its label.
  • Border is the edge line.
  • Margin is transparent space outside the border. It pushes other elements away.

Padding, border, and margin each have four sides. padding: 10px sets all four; padding: 10px 20px sets top and bottom to 10 and left and right to 20; four values go clockwise from the top (padding: 10px 20px 30px 40px is top, right, bottom, left). For one side, use margin-top, padding-left, and so on.

In DevTools, select any element and open the Computed tab (Chrome) or the Layout tab (Firefox). A box-model diagram shows the real numbers for all four layers, and hovering over each layer highlights it on the page.

#How wide is a box, really?

Predict: both boxes below have width: 200px, padding: 20px, and a 5px border. Will they line up with the 200px gray ruler?

By default (box-sizing: content-box), width sets only the content. Padding and border are added on top, so the first box is 5 + 20 + 200 + 20 + 5 = 250px wide and sticks out past the ruler.

With box-sizing: border-box, width means the whole box including padding and border, so the second box is exactly 200px and its content shrinks to 150px. That's far easier to reason about, which is why most projects start their CSS with this rule:

Margin is never part of the width in either mode. It's extra space around the box.

⚠️ Watch out

Vertical margins collapse. When one block sits on top of another, their touching margins don't add up: the bigger one wins. A paragraph with margin-bottom: 30px above one with margin-top: 20px leaves a 30px gap, not 50px. Side-by-side (horizontal) margins and padding never collapse. If spacing looks smaller than you expected, this is usually why.

⚠️ Watch out

Inline elements ignore width and height. <a>, <span>, and <strong> sit inside a line of text, so width, height, and top and bottom margins don't move anything around them. If you need a link to behave like a box (a button, say), give it display: inline-block or display: block.

💡 Tip

To see every box on a page at once, temporarily add * { outline: 2px solid red; }. Unlike a border, an outline takes up no space, so it shows you the layout without changing it.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1The HTML is <p class="tip">Save often</p>. The CSS has .tip { color: green; } first and p { color: purple; } after it. What color is the text?

  • .tip scores 0-1-0 and p scores 0-0-1. Specificity is checked before order, so the class wins even though it comes first.

  • Source order only breaks ties, and these two selectors aren't tied.

  • Both rules target the element directly, so one of them applies.

Show answer

A. .tip scores 0-1-0 and p scores 0-0-1. Specificity is checked before order, so the class wins even though it comes first.

2Two rules both use the selector .button. The first sets background: blue; the second, later in the file, sets background: orange. What color is the button?

  • Earlier never beats later when specificity is equal.

  • Same selector, same specificity, so source order decides and the later rule wins.

  • CSS picks exactly one value per property.

Show answer

B. Same selector, same specificity, so source order decides and the later rule wins.

3A box has width: 300px, padding: 10px, and border: 2px solid, with the default box-sizing. How wide is it on screen, from border edge to border edge?

  • That's the content width only. With the default content-box, padding and border are added on top.

  • That adds one side of padding and border. Both sides count: left and right.

  • 2 + 10 + 300 + 10 + 2 = 324. With border-box it would be exactly 300.

Show answer

C. 2 + 10 + 300 + 10 + 2 = 324. With border-box it would be exactly 300.

4A heading with margin-bottom: 40px sits directly above a paragraph with margin-top: 25px. How big is the gap between them?

  • Vertical margins between stacked blocks don't add up.

  • The margins collapse, and the larger of the two wins.

  • When margins collapse, the larger one is kept, not the smaller.

Show answer

B. The margins collapse, and the larger of the two wins.

Key takeaways

  • A rule is a selector plus declarations. In projects, put CSS in a .css file linked from the <head>.
  • Conflicts are settled by importance, then specificity, then source order. Inherited values lose to anything that targets the element directly.
  • Specificity is IDs-classes-types, compared left to right. Styling with single classes keeps conflicts predictable; avoid IDs and !important for styling.
  • Every box is content, padding, border, and margin. With the default content-box, padding and border add to width; border-box includes them.
  • Vertical margins between stacked blocks collapse to the larger one.

#Further reading

  • Handling conflicts (opens in a new tab): MDN's full explanation of the cascade, specificity, and inheritance, with editable examples.
  • The box model (opens in a new tab): MDN on margins, padding, borders, inline versus block boxes, and margin collapsing.
  • Specificity Calculator (opens in a new tab): type any selector and see its score, a handy way to check your own counting.

m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Link an external stylesheet and organize it into commented sections.
  • Use box-sizing: border-box, padding, borders, and margin: 0 auto to build a centered card.
  • Style labels, inputs, radio buttons, and a button with class and descendant selectors.
  • Diagnose and fix two specificity conflicts by reading selector scores.
  • Add hover, focus, and error states with pseudo-classes, ordered so the right one wins.

Here's the finished card. Click into the fields, hover the button, and type abc into the email box and then click somewhere else.

(The result frame blocks forms from sending, so Sign me up does nothing here. In your own copy with Live Server, it checks the required fields first.)

#Step 1: The files and the HTML

The form uses everything from Module 3: a label for every field, real input types, required, and a <fieldset> for the radio group. Two new details: the radio buttons and checkbox are wrapped inside their labels (the other correct way to pair them), and each field sits in a <div class="field">. That <div> carries no meaning; it's a hook for CSS, which is exactly what <div> is for.

The <link> in the <head> connects css/styles.css. Its path works like an image path: relative to index.html. Create the empty styles.css now. To prove the link works, put body { background: pink; } in it, save, and check the browser. Then delete that line.

#Step 2: A base layer

Start styles.css with rules that affect the whole page:

The first rule switches every element to border-box, so a width always includes padding and border. body loses the browser's default 8px margin and gets padding instead, so the card never touches the screen edge on a phone. system-ui uses the operating system's own font, and line-height: 1.5 spaces lines comfortably. Text properties like color and font-family inherit, so setting them on body styles the whole page at once.

#Step 3: The card

max-width: 420px lets the card shrink on a narrow phone but never grow wider than 420px. margin: 0 auto means "no margin top and bottom, and split the leftover space equally left and right", which centers any block that's narrower than its container.

.card h1 scores 0-1-1, and it only touches headings inside the card. It overrides the browser's default <h1> margin so the heading sits snugly above the intro. Using margins only on the bottom of things, as here, keeps vertical spacing predictable and avoids most margin-collapse surprises.

#Step 4: Labels and text inputs

Labels are inline by default, so display: block puts each one on its own line above its input. The inputs stretch to width: 100% of the card's content area.

font: inherit matters more than it looks. Form controls are an exception to inheritance: browsers give them their own small font, so without this line the text people type is smaller than the rest of the page.

Here's why Step 2's box-sizing rule earns its place. This demo leaves it out. It also starts with <!DOCTYPE html>, so the frame runs in standards mode like your real pages:

The input pokes out of the card. Under content-box, its 100% width is the full content width of the card, and then 24px of padding and 4px of border are added on top. With the reset, those are included in the 100%, and it fits. (Delete the doctype line and the input suddenly fits, because quirks mode, from Module 2, gives inputs border-box. Old browser behavior like that is exactly why the doctype matters.)

#Step 5: Fix the radio buttons (a real specificity bug)

Save and look at the "Which track?" group. Here it is with only the Step 4 rules applied:

Each radio button floats in the middle of its own line above its label, and the answers are bold. Nothing in your CSS asked for that.

Inspect a radio button in DevTools and the Styles pane tells you why: .field input is styling it. The <fieldset> has class="field", so .field input matches the radios inside it, and .field label matches their labels. Your rules reached further than you meant.

The fix is a rule that describes the special case more specifically:

Check the scores. .field .choice (0-2-0) beats .field label (0-1-1) because the middle column is higher. .field .choice input (0-2-1) beats .field input (0-1-1) the same way. Because both fixes win on specificity, they'd work even if you moved them above the rules they override.

A plain .choice (0-1-0) would lose to .field label (0-1-1), wherever you put it. If you try that, DevTools shows font-weight: normal crossed out: the struck-through line is a declaration that lost the cascade. accent-color tints the radio and checkbox to match the button.

#Step 6: The button, and focus you can see

font: inherit comes before font-weight: 700 on purpose. font is a shorthand that resets the weight along with everything else, so the later font-weight line puts bold back. Swap the two lines and the button text goes back to normal weight.

:focus-visible matches when the browser decides a focus ring is needed, which mostly means keyboard users. Press Tab through the finished card at the top of this page: every field and the button light up as you reach them. Never remove focus outlines without replacing them. Keyboard users rely on them to see where they are.

.field input:focus scores 0-2-1, so it beats .field input (0-1-1) no matter where it sits in the file.

#Step 7: An error state, where order decides

:user-invalid matches a field that breaks its rules (empty but required, or an email without an @) after the visitor has interacted with it, so the form doesn't start out covered in red. Browsers older than about 2023 ignore it, and the form still works.

This rule and .field input:focus both score 0-2-1, a tie, so source order decides. With the error rule last, a field that's both focused and invalid shows a red border inside the light focus outline. Put it before the focus rule and the red disappears whenever someone clicks back in to fix the mistake, which is exactly when they need to see it.

#Step 8: Read the cascade in DevTools

Right-click the email field and choose Inspect. In the Styles pane:

  • The strongest rules are listed at the top. Crossed-out declarations lost the cascade to something above them.
  • Use the :hov button (Chrome) or the :hov toggle in Firefox's Rules view to force :focus or :hover on, so you can study those states without holding the mouse still.
  • Select the <main class="card"> and open Computed (Chrome) or Layout (Firefox). The box diagram shows 32px of padding and a 1px border around the content, and the margin on each side is whatever space was left over.

#The finished stylesheet

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does .field input include font: inherit?

  • font has nothing to do with borders.

  • Inputs and buttons get their own font from the browser. font: inherit makes them match the page.

  • Width is a box property and never inherits. width: 100% handles that.

Show answer

B. Inputs and buttons get their own font from the browser. font: inherit makes them match the page.

2Why did the fix for the bold radio labels need .field .choice rather than just .choice?

  • A single class works fine on its own. The problem was what it was competing against.

  • .field .choice scores 0-2-0, which wins on the middle column.

  • The button doesn't have the choice class, so .choice can't select it.

Show answer

B. .field .choice scores 0-2-0, which wins on the middle column.

3Both .field input:focus and .field input:user-invalid set border-color. Why must the :user-invalid rule come last?

  • Pseudo-classes work anywhere in the file.

  • On a specificity tie, source order decides. Last means red wins over the focus color.

  • It has the same specificity as :focus; if it were lower, being later wouldn't help.

Show answer

B. On a specificity tie, source order decides. Last means red wins over the focus color.

Key takeaways

  • Start every stylesheet with the border-box reset, and put page-wide text styles on body so they inherit.
  • max-width plus margin: 0 auto makes a centered card that still shrinks on small screens.
  • Form controls need font: inherit, and focus styles should never be removed without a replacement.
  • When a rule hits more than you meant, inspect the element, read the scores, and write a more specific rule for the special case.
  • On a specificity tie, order decides, so put state rules like errors after the rules they should beat.

  • Add .field input:user-valid { border-color: #16a34a; } so a correctly filled field turns green. Where must it go in the file, and why?
  • Make a .button-secondary class (white background, colored border) for a "Not now" link below the main button, and check that the two button styles don't fight.
