m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write selectors that match exactly the elements you mean, and nothing else.
  • Score and rank selectors by specificity without guessing.
  • Calculate a box's real width under content-box and border-box.
  • Find the usual reasons a CSS rule "does nothing".
  • Control the spacing between stacked boxes, and build a component to an exact size.

Do these in a practice-m4 folder with Live Server running, and keep DevTools open. For every exercise, check your answer in the Styles pane (which rule won, which lines are crossed out) and the Computed box diagram (the real sizes) before opening the solution.

#Warm-up: who wins?

Three rules want to color the same link. Cover the result and predict first.

Orange. .menu a and a.active both score 0-1-1, a tie, so the later one wins. ul li a is last, but it scores only 0-0-3: three type selectors never add up to one class.

#Exercise 1: Write precise selectors

Using this HTML, write one selector for each target. Then give each a different style and check that only its target changes.

  1. Every link in the navigation
  2. Only the current page's link
  3. Only the lead paragraph
  4. The <h1> and the lead paragraph, in one rule
  5. Only the item on sale
  6. Every item in the products list
Need a hint?

Most targets have a class you can use directly. For "every link in the navigation", use a descendant selector that starts from nav. For two targets in one rule, separate the selectors with a comma.

Show solution

For 2, .current is enough on its own; nav .current also works and only matters if the class could appear elsewhere. For 6, .products li reaches every item; plain li would also hit list items anywhere else on a bigger page.

#Exercise 2: Rank by specificity

Score each selector, then sort them from strongest to weakest.

Need a hint?

Count three columns: IDs, then classes and pseudo-classes, then element names. Compare the left column first and only look right when it's tied.

Show solution
Rank Selector Score
1 #main .card 1-1-0
2 .card .title:hover 0-3-0
3 main article .card p 0-1-3
4 .card p 0-1-1
5 article p 0-0-2
6 p 0-0-1

The one ID puts #main .card on top, even though .card .title:hover has three things in the middle column. main article .card p looks long, but its single class ties with .card p, and then its extra element names push it ahead. Check your counting with the Specificity Calculator (opens in a new tab).

#Exercise 3: Measure the boxes

Work out each box's visible width (border edge to border edge), and how much horizontal space it takes up including margins.

  1. width: 250px; padding: 15px; border: 5px solid; margin: 20px; with the default content-box
  2. The same values with box-sizing: border-box. Also: how wide is the content area?
  3. width: 100px; padding: 10px 20px; border: 3px solid; with content-box
Need a hint?

Under content-box, add padding and border on both sides to the width. Under border-box, the width already includes them, so subtract to find the content. Margin sits outside either way. In box 3, which of the two padding values applies to the left and right?

Show solution
  1. Visible: 5 + 15 + 250 + 15 + 5 = 290px. With margins: 20 + 290 + 20 = 330px.
  2. Visible: 250px. Content: 250 − 5 − 15 − 15 − 5 = 210px. With margins: 290px.
  3. padding: 10px 20px means 10 top and bottom, 20 left and right. Visible: 3 + 20 + 100 + 20 + 3 = 146px.

Here are boxes 1 and 2 against a 250px ruler. Select each one in DevTools and compare the Computed diagram with your numbers.

#Exercise 4: Why won't my styles apply?

The goal is a teal-bordered card with a dark orange heading, a crimson note, and bold, 20px paragraph text. None of it works. Find four separate bugs.

Need a hint?

Check four things, one per rule: does the class name match the HTML exactly, including capitals? Is there a dot where a class is meant? Does an earlier rule have a higher score? Does every declaration end with a semicolon?

Show solution
  1. Case. The HTML says class="Card", the CSS says .card. Class names are case-sensitive. Use lowercase in both places.
  2. Missing dot. note looks for a <note> element, which doesn't exist. It should be .note.
  3. An ID wins. #title (1-0-0) beats h2 (0-0-1), so the heading stays navy no matter where the h2 rule goes. Delete the #title rule, or better, don't style with IDs at all.
  4. Missing semicolon. Without the ; after 20px, the browser reads one declaration, font-size: 20px font-weight: bold, which isn't a valid size, and throws the whole thing away. Neither the size nor the bold applies.

In DevTools, an invalid declaration like bug 4 shows up crossed out with a small warning icon, which makes it easy to spot.

#Exercise 5: Fix the spacing

Three notes are stacked inside a bordered panel, each with margin: 24px 0. Predict the gap between two notes, then change the CSS so that:

  • the gap between notes is exactly 16px, and
  • there's no extra space above the first note or below the last one (the panel's own 16px padding is enough).
Need a hint?

The gap between notes is 24px, not 48px: vertical margins collapse. For the fix, give each note margin on one side only, and then remove it from the last note. The pseudo-class :last-child matches an element that's the last child of its parent.

Show solution

Margins only on the bottom means there's nothing to collapse and nothing hanging off the top. .note:last-child scores 0-2-0, so it beats .note (0-1-0) and removes the final margin.

#Exercise 6: A profile card, built to spec

Style this HTML into a card that matches the spec exactly. Use class selectors only.

  • Exactly 300px wide from border edge to border edge, with a 2px border, 12px rounded corners, and 20px of padding.
  • The name has no top margin and 4px of bottom margin; the role is gray with 16px below it.
  • The link looks like a button: white text on a dark background, 8px by 16px of padding, rounded corners, no underline.
  • The link gets darker on hover and shows a clear outline when focused with the keyboard.
Need a hint?

box-sizing: border-box makes "exactly 300px" mean width: 300px. A link is inline, so give it display: inline-block before padding behaves like a button's. You'll need :hover and :focus-visible.

Show solution

The Computed diagram for .profile should read 2 (border) + 20 (padding) + 256 (content) + 20 + 2 = 300. Every selector is a single class, or a class plus a pseudo-class, so nothing scores higher than 0-2-0 and nothing fights.

#Challenge: Put a stylesheet on a specificity diet

Someone styled this alert box with IDs and !important, and now nobody can change it. Rewrite the CSS so it looks the same but uses no IDs and no !important, with no selector scoring above 0-2-0. Then add a second alert with a green "success" look by adding one extra class in the HTML, without touching the original rules.

Need a hint?

Start with a base class (.alert) and a class for its text. For the success version, a "modifier" class like .alert-success that comes later in the file can override colors at equal specificity. The leftover div.alert p rule is dead code: it scores 0-1-2, so the two-ID rule always beat it. Decide whether your version needs it at all.

Show solution

.alert-success ties with .alert at 0-1-0 and comes later, so its border and background win. .alert-success .alert-text (0-2-0) beats .alert-text (0-1-0) for the text color. The old div.alert p rule is gone, because nothing needed it. The margin-bottom is new, only so the two alerts don't touch.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a parent element into a flex container and control its items with justify-content, align-items, gap, and flex-wrap.
  • Explain the main axis and the cross axis, and predict what happens when flex-direction changes.
  • Build grids with grid-template-columns, the fr unit, repeat(), and minmax().
  • Name page regions with grid-template-areas and decide when to reach for Flexbox or Grid.

Put three cards on a page and they stack like pancakes, each one stretched across the whole width. You wanted them side by side. For years, getting there meant floats, clearfix hacks, and a lot of guessing. Today it takes one line of CSS.

Look at the two groups below. The HTML is identical. The only difference is display: flex on the second parent.

#The parent decides the layout

Block elements like <div>, <p>, and <section> follow normal flow: each one starts on a new line and is as wide as its parent. That's why the first group stacks.

When you write display: flex on an element, it becomes a flex container, and its direct children become flex items. The rule goes on the parent, and it only reaches one level down. Grandchildren keep behaving normally unless you make their parent a flex container too.

Notice that the flex cards also shrank to fit their text. Flexbox sizes items by their content first, then hands out leftover space if you ask it to.

#Main axis and cross axis

Every flex container has two directions. The main axis is the direction items line up in. The cross axis runs across it. With the default flex-direction: row, the main axis goes left to right and the cross axis goes top to bottom.

Two properties move items along those axes:

  • justify-content places items along the main axis: flex-start, center, flex-end, space-between, space-around, space-evenly.
  • align-items places items along the cross axis: stretch (the default), flex-start, center, flex-end.

Before you scroll, predict: in the last row, where will the short "A" box sit vertically?

In the default stretch row, A and C grow to match the tallest item, B. With align-items: center, each item keeps its own height and sits in the middle of the cross axis.

🧪 Try it yourself

Copy the preview into your own file and add flex-direction: column to .bar. Now the main axis points down the page, so justify-content moves things vertically and align-items moves them sideways. Give the bar a height: 150px so you can see it.

#Gap, wrapping, and who gets the leftover space

Three more properties handle most real layouts:

  • gap: 12px puts space between items, never on the outside edges. No more margin math.
  • flex-wrap: wrap lets items drop to a new line when they run out of room. Without it, flex items squeeze onto one line, even if that means shrinking below a sensible size.
  • flex: 1 on an item tells it to grow and take whatever space is left over.

Here is a shop toolbar and a list of filter tags using all three.

The search box has flex: 1, so it stretches while the logo and button stay their natural size. The tags wrap onto as many lines as they need, with the same 8px gap between rows and columns.

#Grid: draw the columns first

Flexbox works outward from the content: items take the space they need. Grid works the other way. You describe the columns first, and the items drop into them like eggs into a carton.

grid-template-columns lists one size per column. The fr unit means "a fraction of the free space": the browser subtracts the gaps, then splits what's left into 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 shares. The middle column gets two of them. You can mix units too: grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr gives a fixed sidebar and a main column that takes the rest.

repeat(4, 1fr) is shorthand for 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr. Notice you never wrote any rows: Grid adds them automatically as items run out of columns.

#Columns that count themselves

The nicest trick in Grid is a single line that picks the number of columns for you:

Read it from the inside out. minmax(140px, 1fr) says each column must be at least 140px and may grow to share the free space. auto-fit says "fit as many of those columns as the width allows." Drag the corner of the dashed box below (with a mouse or trackpad) and watch the column count change.

No media queries, no breakpoints. The grid simply responds to the space it's given.

#Name the regions with grid-template-areas

For page layouts, you can draw a little map in your CSS. Each quoted string is one row, and each word names the cell in that column. Then each element claims its region with grid-area.

Writing header twice in the first row makes the header span both columns. To move the sidebar to the right, you'd only change the strings to "main sidebar" and swap the column sizes. The HTML stays put.

#Flexbox or Grid?

Both can do many of the same jobs. Here's a rule of thumb that holds up:

Real pages mix them. A dashboard might use Grid for the whole page (header, sidebar, card area) and Flexbox inside the header to spread out the logo, search box, and profile button. A grid item can be a flex container, and a flex item can be a grid container.

⚠️ Watch out

display: flex on the wrong element. Writing .card { display: flex; } lays out the stuff inside each card, not the cards themselves. To put cards side by side, the rule goes on their parent: .cards { display: flex; }.

⚠️ Watch out

Percent columns plus a gap overflow. grid-template-columns: 33.33% 33.33% 33.33% with gap: 20px is wider than 100%, so the grid sticks out of its container. Use repeat(3, 1fr): fr is measured after the gaps are taken out, so it always fits.

⚠️ Watch out

An area that isn't a rectangle. Every named area in grid-template-areas must form a rectangle, and every row string needs the same number of cells. Break either rule and the browser throws the whole declaration away. In DevTools you'll see the line crossed out with a yellow warning icon, and your items fall back to one column.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You write .card { display: flex; }, but the three .card elements inside .cards still stack on top of each other. Why?

  • row is already the default direction, so adding it changes nothing.

  • The container controls the layout of its direct children. On .card it only arranges what's inside each card.

  • gap only adds space between items that are already laid out by flex or grid.

Show answer

B. The container controls the layout of its direct children. On .card it only arranges what's inside each card.

2A container has display: flex; flex-direction: column;. Which line centers its items horizontally?

  • With column, the main axis runs top to bottom, so this centers items vertically.

  • The cross axis is now horizontal, and align-items works on the cross axis.

  • That centers text inside each item, not the items themselves.

Show answer

B. The cross axis is now horizontal, and align-items works on the cross axis.

3A grid is 600px wide with grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr and no gap. How wide are the columns?

  • That would be 1fr 1fr. The second column gets twice the share.

  • The free space is split into 3 shares of 200px; the first column gets 1, the second gets 2.

  • fr is a share of the free space, not a pixel size.

Show answer

B. The free space is split into 3 shares of 200px; the first column gets 1, the second gets 2.

4Eight cards sit in a 500px wide grid with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)) and no gap. How many columns do you get?

  • Three columns of at least 200px need 600px, which doesn't fit.

  • Two 200px columns fit in 500px, and the 1fr maximum stretches each to 250px to fill the row.

  • Each column must be at least 200px, so eight can't fit side by side.

Show answer

B. Two 200px columns fit in 500px, and the 1fr maximum stretches each to 250px to fill the row.

Key takeaways

  • display: flex and display: grid go on the parent; only its direct children are laid out.
  • In Flexbox, justify-content works along the main axis and align-items along the cross axis. flex-direction: column swaps which way is which.
  • gap spaces items, flex-wrap: wrap lets them break onto new lines, and flex: 1 makes an item take the leftover room.
  • In Grid, fr splits the free space after gaps; repeat(auto-fit, minmax(…, 1fr)) makes a grid that picks its own column count.
  • grid-template-areas draws the page as a map of named rectangles. Use Flexbox for one line of things, Grid for rows and columns, and nest them freely.

#Further reading

  • CSS-Tricks: A Complete Guide to Flexbox (opens in a new tab): every property with a picture, split into "parent" and "children" columns. Worth bookmarking.
  • CSS-Tricks: A Complete Guide to CSS Grid (opens in a new tab): the same format for Grid, including minmax(), auto-fit, and areas.
  • MDN: Basic concepts of flexbox (opens in a new tab): the precise rules for axes, wrapping, and how flex sizes items.

m5-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Mark up a reusable product card with <article>, a heading, a price, and a button.
  • Lay out a set of cards with CSS Grid, then let auto-fit and minmax() choose the column count.
  • Use a column flex container and margin-top: auto to line up buttons across cards of different lengths.
  • Build a wrapping toolbar with justify-content: space-between.

Pixel Pantry, the snack shop from the last lesson, needs a product page. Here is where we're headed: a header with a title and filter buttons, and a grid of cards that rearranges itself to fit any screen. Every "Add to cart" button sits on the same line, no matter how long the description above it is.

Make a new folder called pixel-pantry with an index.html file, and open it with Live Server. Each step below shows the code for that step; type it in, save, and compare your browser with the preview.

#Step 1: Write the HTML for one card

Start with one card and get it right. Everything else is copies.

Why <article>? A product card makes sense on its own, the way a blog post or a comment does, and that's what <article> is for. The <h2> gives each product a real heading, so screen reader users can jump from product to product.

The .thumb div is a stand-in for a photo, so this page works without any image files. In your own shop you'd write <img src="images/mango-chips.jpg" alt="A bowl of orange plantain chips"> instead. The next module shows how to make images like that scale.

#Step 2: Style the card as a box

Add a <style> block (or a styles.css file linked from the <head>) and turn the card into a white box with rounded corners.

Two things to notice. aspect-ratio: 16 / 9 makes the thumbnail's height follow its width, so you never hard-code a height. And the thumbnail is a tiny flex container: align-items and justify-content set to center put the word "Photo" dead center. That's the most common Flexbox job there is.

The max-width: 240px on the card is temporary. Once the grid controls the width, we'll remove it.

#Step 3: Put three cards in a grid

Paste two more cards with different descriptions, wrap all three in a <section class="products">, and give the section a grid.

Delete max-width: 240px from .card now. Here's the result:

It's close, but look at the buttons. They float at different heights because each one sits right under its description. The cards themselves are already equal height (Grid stretches items in a row to match the tallest one), so the fix is to move the buttons, not the cards.

#Step 4: Pin every button to the bottom

Make each card a column flex container, then give the button an automatic top margin:

In a flex container, an auto margin soaks up all the free space on that side. The short popcorn card has lots of spare room, so its button gets a big top margin and drops to the bottom. The long mochi card has none, so its button barely moves. Either way, all three line up.

Notice the button lost width: 100% and still fills the card. In a column flex container, align-items: stretch (the default) stretches every item across the cross axis, which is now horizontal.

#Step 5: Let the grid choose its column count

repeat(3, 1fr) is fine on a laptop, but on a 360px phone each card would be about 100px wide, far too skinny to read. Swap the column rule for the self-counting version:

Now add three more cards so there are six, and drag the dashed frame below to try every width.

Once the frame is narrower than about 430px, two 200px columns plus the gap no longer fit, so the grid drops to one. On a wide screen it fits three or four. You wrote zero media queries.

📝 Note

On a screen narrower than 200px plus padding, minmax(200px, 1fr) would force a column wider than the screen. Pros write minmax(min(200px, 100%), 1fr): min() picks whichever is smaller, so the column never outgrows its container. Kevin Powell explains it in the video below.

#Step 6: Add a toolbar with Flexbox

The header has two groups: a title on the left and filter buttons on the right. That's one row of items, so it's a Flexbox job.

space-between pushes the two groups to opposite ends. flex-wrap: wrap matters on phones: when the title and buttons don't fit on one line, the buttons drop below the title instead of squishing it. The .filters div is its own small flex container, so the buttons stay in a neat row.

The buttons don't filter anything yet. That takes JavaScript, which is a later course. For now they're the layout.

#The finished page

Here is the whole file. Paste it over your index.html and save.

The layout uses exactly three ideas: a Grid for the card area, a column Flexbox inside each card, and a row Flexbox for the toolbar. That combination covers a surprising number of real sites, from online shops to news front pages.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1In Step 4, why does margin-top: auto on the button only work after the card gets display: flex?

  • Buttons accept margins anywhere. The difference is what auto means.

  • In normal flow, a vertical auto margin just becomes 0. Inside a flex container, it absorbs the leftover height and pushes the button down.

  • It pushes the button to the far end. Centering would need auto on both the top and the bottom.

Show answer

B. In normal flow, a vertical auto margin just becomes 0. Inside a flex container, it absorbs the leftover height and pushes the button down.

2Why replace repeat(3, 1fr) with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))?

  • Both rules are just layout. Neither changes loading speed.

  • That's what repeat(3, 1fr) does, and it's the problem on a phone.

  • auto-fit counts the columns from the available width, and 1fr stretches them to fill the row.

Show answer

C. auto-fit counts the columns from the available width, and 1fr stretches them to fill the row.

3Before Step 4, the three cards were already the same height. What caused that?

  • That sets each thumbnail's shape, but the text below still differs in length.

  • Grid items default to stretching across the row, so the short popcorn card grows to match the mochi card.

  • gap only adds space between cards; it never changes their size.

Show answer

B. Grid items default to stretching across the row, so the short popcorn card grows to match the mochi card.

Key takeaways

  • Get one card right first, then copy it. A semantic <article> with an <h2> makes each product easy to find with a screen reader.
  • repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(200px, 100%), 1fr)) gives a card grid that adapts to any width without media queries.
  • A column flex container plus margin-top: auto pins a button to the bottom of a card, so buttons line up across a row.
  • justify-content: space-between with flex-wrap: wrap makes a toolbar that splits to the edges on wide screens and stacks politely on narrow ones.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a "Sold out" card: give it a class that lowers the thumbnail's opacity and add the disabled attribute to its button.
  • Make one product a "Featured" card that spans two columns with grid-column: span 2. Watch what happens to it when the grid drops to one column.
  • Put the price and a small "New" label on the same line using a flex row with justify-content: space-between.
  • Swap the .thumb placeholders for real photos you took, with alt text that describes the snack.

#Further reading

  • web.dev: Learn CSS, Grid (opens in a new tab): Google's course chapter on Grid, with clear diagrams of lines, tracks, and auto-fit.
  • MDN: Basic concepts of grid layout (opens in a new tab): the reference explanation of fr, repeat(), minmax(), and implicit rows.

What you'll learn

  • Pick Flexbox or Grid for a layout problem and explain why.
  • Use flex shorthand, grid-column: span, grid-auto-rows, and grid-template-areas in new situations.
  • Nest a flex container inside a grid to build a real page section.

Each exercise gives you starter HTML and a sketch of the target. Make a file called practice.html, paste the starter in, open it with Live Server, and write the CSS yourself before you peek. When something doesn't move the way you expect, right-click it, choose Inspect, and look for the small flex or grid badge next to the element in the Elements panel. Clicking it draws the lines and gaps right on the page.

#Warm-up: predict the placement

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Without looking at the result, where did box 5 land?

  • Box 4 already took that spot. Each row has only two cells.

  • Two columns per row means boxes 1–2, 3–4, then 5 starts a new row in the first column.

  • Grid creates extra rows automatically; it never drops items.

Show answer

B. Two columns per row means boxes 1–2, 3–4, then 5 starts a new row in the first column.

2What would gap: 6px become if you only wanted space between rows?

  • gap is shorthand for row-gap and column-gap, so you can set either one alone.

  • That spaces the columns apart, which is the opposite of what you wanted.

Show answer

A. gap is shorthand for row-gap and column-gap, so you can set either one alone.

#Exercise 1: Center a badge

A product photo box needs a "Sold out" label in its exact center, both across and down.

Need a hint?

Two properties on .photo handle it with Flexbox: one for each axis. Grid can do it with one property, place-items.

Show solution

display: grid; place-items: center; works too. place-items is shorthand for align-items and justify-items together. Both versions only work because .photo has a height taller than the badge; with no extra space there's nothing to center in.

#Exercise 2: A navigation bar

Put the site name on the far left and the links on the far right, all vertically centered. Remove the list bullets.

Need a hint?

You need two flex containers: the <nav> (two items: the brand and the list) and the <ul> (three items). Lists come with padding and margin you'll want to reset to 0.

Show solution

space-between pushes the brand and the list apart. The <ul> is both a flex item (of the nav) and a flex container (for its links).

#Exercise 3: Footer columns that wrap

A footer has three sections. On a wide screen they sit side by side with equal widths. When there isn't room for each to be at least 180px wide, they wrap onto new lines and fill the row.

Need a hint?

flex takes three values: grow, shrink, and a starting size called the basis. Try flex: 1 1 180px on the sections, and don't forget the container needs to allow wrapping.

Show solution

Each section starts at 180px (the basis), then grows to share any extra space. When three 180px sections plus gaps no longer fit, the last one wraps and grows to fill its own line. This is the Flexbox cousin of auto-fit and minmax(), with one difference: a wrapped item stretches across the whole row instead of lining up with a column above it.

#Exercise 4: A gallery with a featured photo

Make a four-column gallery where every row is 80px tall. The first tile is "featured": it covers two columns and two rows.

Need a hint?

grid-auto-rows sets the height of rows the grid creates by itself. On the featured tile, grid-column: span 2 stretches it across two columns; there's a matching property for rows.

Show solution

The featured tile claims a 2×2 block, and the other tiles flow into the free cells around it, left to right and top to bottom.

#Exercise 5: Rearrange a page without touching the HTML

This page has the menu on the left and the "News" box on the right. Change only grid-template-columns and grid-template-areas so that the menu becomes a strip under the header, and "News" moves to the left of the main content.

Need a hint?

The target has two columns and four rows. Write four strings, each with two names. A name repeated across a row makes that area span the row.

Show solution

Each string is one row, and each word is one column. The HTML order never changed, which is the point: Grid lets you redraw the page in CSS. One caution for later: keyboard users still move through elements in HTML order, so keep the visual order close to the source order.

#Exercise 6: A dashboard with a toolbar and stat cards

This is the module's big one, and it mixes everything. Build a dashboard with:

  1. A 200px sidebar on the left and the main area on the right (Grid).
  2. A toolbar at the top of the main area with the page title on the left and a search box plus a button on the right (Flexbox). The search box should grow to fill spare space.
  3. Stat cards that fit as many columns as possible, each at least 140px wide (Grid with auto-fit).
Need a hint?

Work from the outside in. Style .dash first and check the two columns. Then .toolbar with space-between, then .tools as its own flex row where the input gets flex: 1. For the input to grow, .tools itself needs to grow too.

Show solution

Three layouts are nested here: a Grid for the page, a Flexbox row for the toolbar (with another inside it for the tools), and an auto-fit Grid for the cards. min-width: 0 on the input matters. Form fields have a built-in minimum width, and without that line the input refuses to shrink on narrow screens and pushes the button off the edge.

#Challenge: A month calendar

Build a calendar for a month that starts on a Wednesday and has 30 days. Use a 7-column grid with a row of day names (Sun to Sat) on top. Day 1 must sit under "Wed", and day 18 should be highlighted as today. Use only one placement rule for day 1, and let everything else flow.

Need a hint?

Every cell can be a plain <div>, including the day names. Day 1 needs to start in the fourth column; look up grid-column-start.

Show solution

Once day 1 starts in column 4, the browser fills the rest of the row and wraps day 5 to the next line on its own. To change months, you change one number.

💡 Tip

Want more reps? Flexbox Froggy (opens in a new tab) and Grid Garden (opens in a new tab) are free browser games where each level is one layout puzzle. Most people finish both in an afternoon.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Add the viewport meta tag and explain what goes wrong without it.
  • Choose between px, %, rem, and vw, and size text with clamp().
  • Write mobile-first CSS with min-width media queries, and make images shrink to fit.
  • Check text contrast, keep visible focus styles, support keyboard users, and respect prefers-reduced-motion.

Maya's portfolio looks great on her laptop. Her friend opens the link on a phone and has to pinch to read anything, and the project gallery runs off the right edge. Another visitor, who uses the keyboard instead of a mouse, presses Tab and can't tell where they are on the page, because Maya wrote outline: none to get rid of "that ugly blue ring."

A missing tag, one fixed width, and one line of CSS caused all three. Each has a small fix.

#The viewport tag comes first

Phones still have to show old sites built for desktops. So unless a page says otherwise, many mobile browsers lay it out in a pretend window about 980px wide, then shrink the result to fit. Everything becomes tiny, and your phone-sized CSS never runs.

This line in the <head> tells the browser to use the device's real width:

VS Code's ! shortcut for a new HTML file adds it for you.

#Sizes that bend instead of break

Maya's gallery had width: 900px. On a 390px phone, that's 510px of sideways scrolling. Here are the units to reach for instead:

Unit Means Good for
px a fixed size borders, small details
% a share of the parent's size widths inside a container
rem a multiple of the root font size (16px by default) font sizes, spacing
vw 1% of the viewport's width fluid sizes, used inside clamp()

Use rem for text. Some visitors raise the default font size in their browser settings because they need bigger text. Sizes in rem grow with that setting; sizes in px ignore it.

Two patterns fix most width problems. max-width lets an element shrink but caps how wide it gets. And clamp(min, preferred, max) picks the preferred value but never goes below the minimum or above the maximum.

The heading's size is 1rem + 4vw, so it grows as the screen widens, but clamp() holds it between 1.75rem and 3rem. On a phone it won't shrink to nothing, and on a giant monitor it won't turn into a billboard. The margin: 0 auto centers the box once it hits its max width.

#Mobile-first media queries

Sometimes the layout itself has to change: a sidebar sits beside the content on a laptop but below it on a phone. Media queries are CSS that only applies when a condition is true.

The smart way to use them is mobile-first. Write your normal CSS for the smallest screen, usually one simple column. Then add min-width queries that layer on columns as space appears. Small screens get the simplest CSS, and you rarely undo anything.

In the preview below, the frame is the viewport. Read the width it reports, then predict: one column or two?

On a laptop the frame is wider than 600px, so you see two columns. On a phone you see one. To watch it switch in your own project, open Chrome DevTools and press Ctrl+Shift+M (Cmd+Shift+M on a Mac) to toggle the device toolbar, then drag the width or pick a preset like Mobile M (375px).

#Images that shrink to fit

A photo straight off a phone camera can be 4000px wide. By default an <img> shows at its real size, so one big photo can break the whole layout. One rule fixes it everywhere:

The first image pokes far out of its 260px box. The second shrinks to fit, and height: auto keeps its shape. Put img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } near the top of every stylesheet, and keep the width and height attributes in your HTML so the browser can reserve space before the image loads.

#Remove the barriers you can't see

A page that fits every screen can still shut people out. Five checks catch most problems.

Contrast. Light grey on white looks elegant and is hard to read, especially on a phone in sunlight. The accessibility guidelines (WCAG) ask for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (about 24px, or 18.5px bold).

Check any pair with the WebAIM contrast checker, or click a color swatch in DevTools' Styles pane, where Chrome shows the contrast ratio.

Visible focus. When someone presses Tab, the browser outlines the element that has focus. Removing that outline is like hiding the mouse pointer. If you don't like the default ring, replace it; never just delete it. :focus-visible matches when the browser decides a focus ring is useful (keyboard use), so mouse clicks don't trigger it.

Real controls. Tab only stops on focusable things: links with an href, buttons, and form fields. A <div> with a click handler can't be reached. Click the first line of the preview below, then press Tab a few times and watch where focus goes.

Focus lands on the first link with no visible sign, then the second link shows a clear ring, then it jumps straight past the fake button to the real one. Keyboard users never learn the fake one exists.

Alt text. Every <img> needs an alt that says what the image tells the reader. Pure decoration gets alt="", so screen readers skip it.

Motion. Some people get dizzy or sick from animation. Operating systems have a "reduce motion" setting, and CSS can read it:

To test it without changing your computer's settings, open the DevTools Command Menu (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P), run Show Rendering, and set Emulate CSS media feature prefers-reduced-motion to reduce.

⚠️ Watch out

outline: none with nothing to replace it. This one line makes a site unusable for keyboard users, and it hides in a lot of copied CSS. Search your stylesheet for outline: none and outline: 0, and wherever you find one, add a :focus-visible rule with an outline that has at least 3:1 contrast against the background.

⚠️ Watch out

Max-width and min-width queries fighting. With both @media (max-width: 600px) and @media (min-width: 600px) in one file, both apply at exactly 600px. Go mobile-first and use min-width everywhere.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A page looks tiny and zoomed-out on every phone, and none of its media queries seem to run. What's the most likely cause?

  • rem works fine in media queries. The queries never match because the browser thinks the screen is wide.

  • Without it, many phones lay the page out about 980px wide and shrink it, so phone-sized queries never apply.

  • That would cause overflowing images, not a zoomed-out page with dead media queries.

Show answer

B. Without it, many phones lay the page out about 980px wide and shrink it, so phone-sized queries never apply.

2Mobile-first CSS puts the phone layout in the base styles. Which media query adds a two-column layout for wider screens?

  • The rules apply once the screen is at least 40rem wide, adding columns on top of the one-column base.

  • That applies to small screens, which is desktop-first thinking.

  • That only matches a screen exactly 40rem wide.

Show answer

A. The rules apply once the screen is at least 40rem wide, adding columns on top of the one-column base.

3What does font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 5vw, 3rem) give on a 400px-wide phone?

  • 5vw is 20px here, but that's below the minimum.

  • 5% of 400px is 20px, which is under the 1.5rem floor, so the floor wins.

  • The maximum only applies once 5vw passes 48px, at 960px wide.

Show answer

B. 5% of 400px is 20px, which is under the 1.5rem floor, so the floor wins.

4A designer builds a "button" as <div class="btn" onclick="buy()">Buy</div>. What happens for someone using only a keyboard?

  • Enter only activates elements that can take focus, and a plain div can't.

  • A div isn't focusable. Using <button type="button"> gives you focus, Enter, and Space for free.

  • A focus style only shows on elements that can receive focus.

Show answer

B. A div isn't focusable. Using <button type="button"> gives you focus, Enter, and Space for free.

Key takeaways

  • Every page needs <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">.
  • Avoid fixed widths. Use max-width, %, and rem, and size headings with clamp(min, preferred, max).
  • Mobile-first: base CSS is the one-column phone layout; @media (min-width: …) adds columns as screens grow.
  • img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } stops images from breaking layouts.
  • 4.5:1 contrast, a visible :focus-visible style, real <a> and <button> elements, useful alt text, and a prefers-reduced-motion rule remove the most common barriers.

#Further reading

  • MDN: Responsive design (opens in a new tab): the full tour, including the history of why the viewport tag exists.
  • web.dev: Learn Accessibility (opens in a new tab): a free course from Google; the chapters on focus, color and contrast, and keyboard access fit right after this lesson.
  • WebAIM Contrast Checker (opens in a new tab): paste two colors and get the ratio with a pass or fail for each WCAG level.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Start a page with the viewport tag and write its base CSS for phones first.
  • Size the page with min(), clamp(), and rem, and make the hero image scale.
  • Add one min-width media query that turns the hero into two columns.
  • Add a skip link, visible focus styles, checked contrast, and a reduced-motion rule, then test at phone, tablet, and laptop widths.

The Starfield Club runs free telescope nights at a high school, and they need a page people can open from a flyer's QR code. That means most visitors arrive on a phone. Here's the finished page. If you're on a laptop, the hero shows two columns; on a phone, it's one.

There's also a hidden "Skip to main content" link at the very top that only appears for keyboard users. You'll add it in Step 6 and try it there.

Make a folder called starfield with index.html, styles.css, and an images folder, and open index.html with Live Server.

#Step 1: The HTML, with the viewport tag

Write the whole structure first, with no CSS at all. You've seen most of these elements before: a <header> with a <nav>, a <main> with three <section>s, and a <footer>.

For the image, save this small drawing as images/saturn.svg. SVG files are just text, so you can paste it straight into VS Code.

Three details matter for later steps. The id="main" on <main> is where the skip link jumps. The width and height on the <img> let the browser reserve space for it. And every section's content sits inside a .wrap, which will control the page width in one place.

#Step 2: Base styles for the smallest screen

Open styles.css. Everything you write before any media query is the phone layout.

Read the .wrap rule out loud: "be the smaller of full width minus 2rem or 64rem." On a phone, the first value wins, leaving 1rem of breathing room on each side. On a laptop, 64rem (1024px) wins, and margin: 0 auto centers it. One line replaces a fixed width, a max-width, and side padding.

#Step 3: A header and hero that work at 360px

Here is the header and hero with only the base and Step 3 styles. There's no media query yet, so you're looking at the phone layout even on a wide screen: text first, image underneath.

(The preview caps the image at 420px so it fits on this page. Your version can leave that out.)

The header is the toolbar pattern from the last module: space-between with flex-wrap, so on a very narrow phone the links drop under the club name instead of overlapping it. gap: 0.5rem 1.5rem sets a smaller gap between rows than between columns.

.hero-row is a grid with no columns declared, which means one column: text, then image. We'll add the second column in Step 5. The heading uses clamp() so it's 2rem on a small phone and grows to 3.5rem at most.

The "Save a spot" link is styled as a button, but it's still an <a>, because it takes you somewhere. Use <a> for going places and <button> for doing things, and keyboards and screen readers will treat each one correctly.

#Step 4: Feature cards and the sign-up row

The feature cards are the self-counting grid from the product page, so they're already responsive. The email row uses flex: 1 1 14rem: the input wants to be 14rem wide and grows to fill the row; when the row is too narrow for the input and the button side by side, the button wraps underneath. font: inherit matters because form controls don't inherit the page font by default.

#Step 5: One media query for wider screens

Here is the only media query on the page:

At 40rem (640px) and up, the hero gets more breathing room and splits into text on the left and image on the right. Everything else already adapts by itself, thanks to min(), clamp(), auto-fit, and flex-wrap. That's the goal of a good responsive page: let flexible units do most of the work and save media queries for the few changes they can't make.

#Step 6: The accessibility pass

Try the skip link and both focus colors here. Click the line of text at the top, then press Tab slowly. (In this demo the hint sits above the skip link so your first Tab reaches it; on a real page the skip link comes first.)

The skip link is the first thing in the page. It's parked off-screen until it gets focus, then slides into view. A keyboard user can press Enter to jump past the header straight to <main>, instead of tabbing through every nav link on every page.

Focus styles use two colors: dark blue on the white parts of the page, and yellow on the dark header and hero, so the ring always stands out.

Contrast was checked for every text color. White heading text on #0f172a is about 18 to 1, the dark text on the yellow button is 10.7 to 1, and the grey #475569 card text on its light background is 6.9 to 1. All pass the 4.5 to 1 minimum with room to spare.

Motion is opt-in. Smooth scrolling and the button's small lift only switch on inside prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference, so anyone who has asked their device to reduce motion never gets them.

#Step 7: Test it like a visitor

  1. Phone, tablet, laptop. Open DevTools, toggle the device toolbar (Ctrl+Shift+M, or Cmd+Shift+M on a Mac), and try the Mobile M, Tablet, and Laptop width presets. Look for sideways scrolling, text that's too small, and things that overlap.
  2. Keyboard only. Put the mouse away. Press Tab from the top: the skip link should appear first, then the club name, the nav links, the "Save a spot" button, the email field, and the "Join the list" button, in that order, each with a visible ring.
  3. Zoom to 200%. Press Ctrl and + (or Cmd and +) until the zoom reads 200%. Nothing should be cut off, and you shouldn't need to scroll sideways.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the page use width: min(100% - 2rem, 64rem) on .wrap instead of width: 64rem?

  • It's a sizing rule only; loading speed doesn't change.

  • min() picks the smaller value at every width, so the box shrinks on phones and stops growing on laptops.

  • margin: 0 auto does the centering. min() only chooses the width.

Show answer

B. min() picks the smaller value at every width, so the box shrinks on phones and stops growing on laptops.

2The smooth scrolling and hover lift sit inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference). What does that achieve?

  • People who haven't changed the setting still get the motion.

  • The default is no motion, and the effects are added only when the visitor has no preference against them.

  • The query reads an accessibility setting, not the screen size.

Show answer

B. The default is no motion, and the effects are added only when the visitor has no preference against them.

3"Save a spot" looks like a button. Why is it written as an <a> instead of a <button>?

  • Screen readers announce it as a link, and it supports opening in a new tab and other link behavior.

  • Buttons can be styled just like links.

  • Buttons and form fields are focusable too.

Show answer

A. Screen readers announce it as a link, and it supports opening in a new tab and other link behavior.

Key takeaways

  • Base CSS is the phone layout. Here, one min-width media query was the only one the page needed.
  • width: min(100% - 2rem, 64rem); margin: 0 auto; is a reusable page container that fits every screen.
  • Flexible pieces such as clamp() headings, auto-fit grids, and wrapping flex rows adapt without breakpoints.
  • A skip link, focus styles that contrast with every background, checked text contrast, and opt-in motion make the page usable for keyboard users and people sensitive to animation.
  • Test at three widths, with the keyboard alone, and at 200% zoom before you call a page done.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a "Next three nights" section with a small table of dates, and make sure it doesn't overflow at 360px. (Hint: wrap it in a div with overflow-x: auto.)
  • Add a second media query at 64rem that shows the feature cards in exactly three columns.
  • Make the nav links bigger touch targets by giving them padding, so they're easy to tap on a phone.
  • Try a light theme for the hero, then re-check every contrast ratio with the WebAIM checker.

#Further reading

  • web.dev: Responsive web design basics (opens in a new tab): Google's guide to the viewport, flexible content, and choosing breakpoints by content instead of by device.
  • Chrome DevTools: Simulate mobile devices with device mode (opens in a new tab): every option in the device toolbar, including throttling and width presets.

m6-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Find and fix the CSS that causes sideways scrolling and unreadable text on phones.
  • Convert desktop-first CSS into mobile-first CSS.
  • Repair focus styles, contrast, keyboard access, and motion problems in someone else's code.

Every exercise here is a page that's already broken in a way real sites are. Read the starter, predict what's wrong, then fix it in your own practice.html with Live Server running. Keep DevTools open with the device toolbar on (Ctrl+Shift+M or Cmd+Shift+M) and set it to 375px wide, the width of a common phone.

#Warm-up: which line breaks the phone layout?

Check your understanding

1 question

1On a 375px phone, which rule makes the page scroll sideways?

  • max-width only caps the width; on a phone the box simply shrinks.

  • 100% follows the parent, so it can't be wider than its container.

  • Three fixed 300px columns need at least 900px, no matter how narrow the screen is.

  • clamp() keeps the font between 1.5rem and 3rem; it never forces extra width.

Show answer

C. Three fixed 300px columns need at least 900px, no matter how narrow the screen is.

#Exercise 1: Stop the sideways scroll

This "About me" page has a fixed width. Unless your screen is very wide, the preview below already shows a horizontal scrollbar. Fix it so the box is never wider than 900px, never wider than the screen, and always keeps at least 1rem of space at each edge.

Need a hint?

You need the smaller of two widths: the screen minus some room, or 900px. There's a CSS function named after exactly that.

Show solution

max-width: 900px with margin: 0 1rem gets you close too, but the margins fight with margin: 0 auto for centering. min() does both jobs in one line. box-sizing: border-box stops the padding from making the box wider than the width you set.

#Exercise 2: A heading that grows, within limits

Write a font-size for an <h1> that is never smaller than 2rem, never larger than 4rem, and otherwise equals 5vw. Then answer: at what screen widths does it stop shrinking and stop growing? (1rem is 16px.)

Need a hint?

clamp(min, preferred, max). For the widths, ask: when does 5% of the screen width equal 32px? When does it equal 64px?

Show solution

5vw equals 2rem (32px) when the screen is 640px wide, because 5% of 640 is 32. It equals 4rem (64px) at 1280px. So the heading is fixed at 32px on phones, grows smoothly between 640px and 1280px, and stops at 64px on big monitors.

Pure vw has one problem: if a visitor zooms in, vw text doesn't get bigger, because the viewport didn't change. Mixing in rem, as in clamp(2rem, 1rem + 4vw, 4rem), keeps part of the size tied to the visitor's font setting.

#Exercise 3: Flip it to mobile-first

This CSS was written desktop-first. Rewrite it so the base styles are for phones and the only media query uses min-width. The page must look the same at every width as before.

Need a hint?

Take whatever is inside the max-width query and make it the base. Then the old base values move into a min-width query that starts where the old one ended.

Show solution

Below 48rem you get one column with no sidebar; at 48rem and up you get three columns and the sidebar. The base grid-template-columns: 1fr isn't strictly needed, since a grid with no columns has one, but writing it makes the intent obvious.

Hiding the sidebar on phones is a content choice, not a CSS one. If it holds something useful, a better phone layout moves it below the main content instead of removing it.

#Exercise 4: Bring back the focus ring

Someone added the first line of this stylesheet "to clean up the design." Click the first line of the preview and press Tab: you can't see where you are. Fix it so keyboard users get a clear ring that has at least 3:1 contrast against both the white page and the dark button, without showing a ring when someone clicks with a mouse.

Need a hint?

Delete the bad line, then style :focus-visible. An outline-offset puts a gap between the element and its ring, so the ring sits on the page background instead of on the button.

Show solution

#1d4ed8 on white is 6.7:1. Thanks to the 3px offset, the ring around the button is drawn on the white page, not on the dark button, so it only has to contrast with white. Mouse users who click the button don't see a ring, because browsers don't match :focus-visible for most mouse clicks on buttons.

#Exercise 5: Fix the contrast

This sale card fails contrast in two places. Measure both with the WebAIM Contrast Checker (opens in a new tab), then pick new colors that pass 4.5:1 while keeping the same feel (grey text, blue button).

Need a hint?

The grey text and the white-on-light-blue button are the two problems. In the checker, darken the color with the slider until both "Normal Text" results say Pass.

Show solution

The original grey #9ca3af on white is 2.5:1, and white on #60a5fa is also 2.5:1. Both fail.

#4b5563 on white is 7.6:1, and white on #2563eb is 5.2:1. Both pass with a margin, and the card still reads as "soft grey and blue." The light border #e5e7eb is fine to leave faint, because it's decoration: nobody needs to see it to use the card.

#Exercise 6: A fake button and a restless badge

This page has two problems. The "Like" control is a <div>, so keyboard users can't reach it. And the red "LIVE" badge pulses forever, even for people who have asked their device to reduce motion. Fix both. The like count should still go up on click, and now also on Enter and Space.

Need a hint?

Changing one tag name gives you focus, Enter, and Space for free. For the badge, write a media query that switches the animation off when the visitor prefers reduced motion.

Show solution

A <button> is focusable and fires its click handler on Enter and Space, so the same onclick now works from the keyboard. The font: inherit and background lines make the button look like the old div. To test the badge fix, use DevTools' Show Rendering command and set the reduced-motion emulation to reduce; the pulsing stops.

#Challenge: A gallery that works everywhere

Build an art club gallery with six pieces. Each piece is a card with an image, a title, and the artist's name, and the whole card is a link to that piece's page. It must:

  1. Show one column on phones, two at 40rem, and three at 64rem, written mobile-first.
  2. Give every image the same 4:3 shape without stretching it, even if the original is tall or wide.
  3. Show a clear focus ring around the whole card when it's tabbed to.
  4. Zoom the image slightly on hover, but only for visitors who haven't asked for reduced motion.
  5. Use alt text that describes each artwork.
Need a hint?

aspect-ratio: 4 / 3 and object-fit: cover on the image give you same-shape images that are cropped, not squashed. Put the <a> around the card's contents and style .card:focus-visible. Wrap the hover transform in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference).

Show solution

Two cards are shown here; the other four follow the same pattern. The colored SVGs stand in for real artwork.

The tall purple image and the wide teal one end up the same shape: aspect-ratio sets the box, and object-fit: cover fills it by cropping the edges instead of squashing the picture. overflow: hidden on the card keeps the zoomed image inside the rounded corners. The gallery is a <ul>, so screen readers can announce it as a list of six items before the visitor starts. Some browsers, Safari in particular, stop treating a list as a list once its bullets are removed with list-style: none, which is why the <ul> also has role="list".

m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Use size, weight, color, and spacing to show readers what matters most.
  • Set readable body text with a type scale, line height, and line length.
  • Store colors, sizes, and spacing in CSS custom properties and reuse them with var().
  • Write relative links between pages in different folders, and link one stylesheet from every page.

Lena built her club's website one page at a time. The home page used #2563eb for links, the events page used royalblue, and the join page used whatever VS Code's color picker landed on. Headings were 28px on one page and 2em on another. Each page looked fine alone. Together they looked like three different websites, and visitors clicking "Events" thought they'd left the site.

#Hierarchy: what should people see first?

Visitors don't read a page top to bottom. They scan, looking for the part they care about. Visual hierarchy is how you guide that scan: the most important thing looks the most important.

Both cards below have the same words. Squint at them until the text blurs. On which one can you still tell what's going on?

The left card makes everything bold, so nothing stands out. The right one uses four tools you'll use on every page:

  • Size: the headline is the biggest thing.
  • Weight and case: the small uppercase label says "category" without competing with the headline.
  • Color: the paragraph is a softer grey, and the one action gets the strongest color on the card.
  • Spacing: the label sits close to the headline it belongs to, and there's more room above the button.

#Type that's easy to read

Good body text is mostly a few numbers set well:

The ch unit is the width of the "0" character, so 65ch keeps lines around 65 characters. Much longer, and the eye loses its place finding the next line.

For heading sizes, don't pick numbers one at a time. Use a type scale: start at the body size and multiply by the same ratio for each step. With a ratio of 1.25:

Step Size Use
0 1rem (16px) body text
1 1.25rem (20px) h3, lead paragraph
2 1.563rem (25px) h2
3 1.953rem (31px) h1 on inner pages
4 2.441rem (39px) the home page headline

Because every size comes from one ratio, the headings look related.

#A spacing scale, and why closeness means "related"

Spacing works the same way. Pick a short list of sizes, such as 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, and 3rem, and use only those. Pages built from one list feel calm, even if visitors can't say why.

To choose which size, use proximity: things that belong together sit closer together. A heading should be nearer to its own paragraph than to the section above it.

#Color with a job

A site needs fewer colors than you'd think, and each one should have a job: a dark text color on a light background, a slightly different surface for cards, and one brand color for links and main buttons so visitors can spot what's clickable. An accent for small badges is optional. Check every text and background pair for 4.5:1 contrast; a color can be on-brand and still fail.

#Custom properties: decide once, use everywhere

Lena's bug was typing the same decision many times. CSS custom properties (often called CSS variables) let you type it once:

A custom property's name starts with two dashes. You set it like any property, and you read it with var(). Properties set on :root (the <html> element) are inherited by the whole page. Change #1d4ed8 in one place, and every link, button, and border that uses it changes too.

They also follow the cascade. Set new values on a class, and everything inside that element uses them. Press the button:

The .night rule redefines four colors on <body>, and every rule that reads them updates at once. None of the card's CSS changed.

#Many pages, one site

A multi-page site is just a folder of HTML files that link to each other. Here's a typical layout:

Links between them use relative paths: directions starting from the file you're in.

From To href
index.html events.html events.html
index.html css/styles.css css/styles.css
index.html projects/robot-arm.html projects/robot-arm.html
projects/robot-arm.html index.html ../index.html
projects/robot-arm.html css/styles.css ../css/styles.css

A folder name followed by / means "go into this folder." ../ means "go up one folder." That's the whole system.

Three habits keep the pages consistent:

  1. One stylesheet. Every page links css/styles.css (with ../ in front for pages in subfolders), and no page has its own <style> block.
  2. The same header. Copy the exact same <header> and <nav> onto every page, so the menu never moves.
  3. Mark where the visitor is. Add aria-current="page" to the nav link for the current page. Screen readers announce "current page," and [aria-current="page"] lets you style it.

⚠️ Watch out

Links that start with /. href="/css/styles.css" means "from the very top of the website," not "from this folder." On a GitHub Pages project site, the top is username.github.io, not your project folder, so the styles vanish. Use relative paths like css/styles.css.

⚠️ Watch out

Capital letters in file names. Windows and macOS usually treat About.html and about.html as the same file, so a mismatched link works on your laptop. GitHub Pages treats them as different, and the link gives a 404 once you publish. Name every file and folder in lowercase, with dashes instead of spaces.

⚠️ Watch out

A typo in a variable name fails silently. color: var(--colour-brand) (British spelling) refers to a property that doesn't exist. No error appears; the color quietly falls back to the inherited value. If a style isn't applying, hover over the var() in DevTools' Styles pane: it shows the value, or flags the name as not defined.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A page at events/spring.html needs the stylesheet at css/styles.css (both inside the site's main folder). What goes in href?

  • That would look for events/css/styles.css, a folder that doesn't exist.

  • ../ climbs out of events/ to the main folder, and css/styles.css goes from there.

  • That starts from the top of the whole website, which breaks when the site lives in a subfolder.

Show answer

B. ../ climbs out of events/ to the main folder, and css/styles.css goes from there.

2:root sets --color-brand: blue, and .promo sets --color-brand: orange. A button inside .promo uses background: var(--color-brand). What color is it?

  • :root sets the default, but a closer ancestor's value wins, just like inheritance.

  • The button inherits --color-brand from its nearest ancestor that sets it, which is .promo.

  • Redefining a custom property in a smaller scope is allowed and is how themes work.

Show answer

B. The button inherits --color-brand from its nearest ancestor that sets it, which is .promo.

3Every paragraph on a page is bold, 18px, and the same color as the headings. What's the most direct fix for the hierarchy?

  • Bigger text that's all the same still has no hierarchy.

  • Hierarchy comes from contrast between levels, so headings need to be the only big, bold text.

  • More colors without a job create noise, not hierarchy.

Show answer

B. Hierarchy comes from contrast between levels, so headings need to be the only big, bold text.

4Why set max-width: 65ch on paragraphs?

  • ch only sets a width, and phones are usually narrower than 65 characters anyway.

  • Very long lines make readers lose their place.

  • Centering needs margin: 0 auto. max-width only caps the width.

Show answer

B. Very long lines make readers lose their place.

Key takeaways

  • Hierarchy comes from four tools: size, weight, color, and spacing. Squint at a page to test it.
  • Body text: 1rem, line height around 1.6, lines around 65ch. Headings come from one type scale.
  • Use a short spacing scale, and put related things closer together than unrelated ones.
  • Store design decisions in custom properties on :root, read them with var(), and override them on a class for variations.
  • Pages connect with relative paths like ../index.html. Every page links one stylesheet, repeats one header, and marks its nav link with aria-current="page".

#Further reading

  • MDN: Using CSS custom properties (opens in a new tab): the details on inheritance, fallback values like var(--x, blue), and what happens with invalid values.
  • web.dev: Learn CSS, Typography (opens in a new tab): line height, line length, font stacks, and more, with live examples.
  • MDN: Dealing with files (opens in a new tab): how to name and organize a website's files, including why spaces and capitals cause trouble.

Riverside Robotics, the club whose navbar you built in the layout practice, wants a real website: a home page, an events page, and a sign-up page. The rule for this build is that no page gets its own styles. Every color, size, and gap comes from one file, so the three pages can't drift apart the way Lena's did.

Here's the home page you'll finish with. The events and join pages use the same header, footer, and stylesheet.

#Step 1: Make the folders and files

In VS Code, open an empty folder called riverside-robotics (File > Open Folder). Use the New File and New Folder buttons at the top of the Explorer to make this structure:

All names are lowercase with no spaces, so they'll work the same once the site is online. The stylesheet lives in its own folder, which keeps the main folder tidy as the site grows.

#Step 2: Write the design tokens

Open css/styles.css. Before writing a single selector, write down every design decision as a custom property on :root:

The type sizes are the 1.25 scale from the notes. The spacing names (2xs up to xl) are like t-shirt sizes, so you can tell at a glance that --space-m is bigger than --space-s. From here on, the rule is simple: if you're about to type a color, a font size, or a margin, use a token instead.

The colors were checked before they went in. --color-brand (#0f766e) on white is 5.5:1, and on the grey --color-surface it's 5.0:1, so it's safe for links, labels, and button backgrounds. --color-muted text is 7.6:1 on white.

#Step 3: Base styles for every page

Add these under the tokens. They style plain HTML elements, so they apply on every page without any classes.

Here's what those base styles do to plain HTML, with no classes at all:

Every heading size, line height, and gap came from a token. The :focus-visible rule is in the base on purpose: it covers every link and button on every page, so you can't forget it on page three.

#Step 4: One header for every page

This is the header HTML. It goes at the top of <body> on all three pages, and only the position of aria-current="page" changes from page to page.

And its styles, plus the footer's:

Here it is as it appears on the events page, with aria-current moved to the Events link:

Two details. The selector a[aria-current="page"] styles the current link using the same attribute that screen readers read, so the visual cue and the spoken cue can never disagree. And every nav link has a 3px transparent bottom border. The current link just changes the border's color, so links don't jump up and down by 3px when you switch pages.

#Step 5: Components you'll reuse

Now the pieces that appear on more than one page: the small label above headings, the large intro paragraph, the button, the card grid, and the form layout. Add them along with the layout rules and the one media query.

Notice there's only one media query, and it only bumps the h1 up one step on wider screens. Everything else (the header, the card grid, the page width) already adapts on its own, using the patterns from the last module.

#Step 6: Build the three pages

The home page. Here is the complete index.html. The <link> in the <head> is the line that connects it to the stylesheet.

The events page. Copy index.html and save the copy as events.html. Change exactly three things: the <title> to Events | Riverside Robotics, the aria-current="page" (move it to the Events link), and everything inside <main>:

The previews on this page include a few lines of preview-only script that stop the links from leaving the frame. Your real files don't need it.

  1. Open index.html with Live Server. Click every link in the nav on every page. Each one should load, and the underline should move to the page you're on.
  2. If a page shows up as plain black text on white, its <link> path is wrong. Open DevTools and look at the Console: you'll see a red 404 (Not Found) error naming the file it couldn't find.
  3. Now the payoff. In styles.css, change --color-brand from #0f766e to #6d28d9 and save. Click through all three pages: links, labels, buttons, focus rings, and the current-page underline all turned purple at once. (That purple is 7.1:1 on white, so it passes too.)

That one-line change is the whole reason for tokens. A site with a hundred pages works exactly the same way.

#The finished stylesheet

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does every nav link have border-bottom: 3px solid transparent, even though you can't see it?

  • An invisible border has no effect on contrast.

  • If only the current link had a border, it would be 3px taller than the others, and the nav would jump between pages.

  • Links with an href are focusable on their own.

Show answer

B. If only the current link had a border, it would be 3px taller than the others, and the nav would jump between pages.

2You add a page at projects/robot-arm.html, inside a new folder. What has to change in its copy of the header and <head>?

  • The header is identical in what it shows, but paths are relative to the file's location.

  • The page is one folder deeper, so each relative path has to climb up one level first.

  • The nav links would break too: index.html would point to projects/index.html.

Show answer

B. The page is one folder deeper, so each relative path has to climb up one level first.

3The button's text color uses var(--color-on-brand) instead of writing white. What does that buy you?

  • They give the same color today. The difference shows up when you change the design.

  • Every button, badge, or banner that sits on the brand color reads the same token, so they all stay readable together.

  • Custom properties don't change loading speed.

Show answer

B. Every button, badge, or banner that sits on the brand color reads the same token, so they all stay readable together.

Key takeaways

  • Plan the folders first, with lowercase names and a separate css/ folder.
  • Write tokens on :root before any selectors, check their contrast once, and never type a raw color or size again.
  • Base styles on plain elements (body, h1, p, a, :focus-visible) give every page the same typography for free.
  • Copy one header onto every page and move only aria-current="page". Style the current link with an attribute selector so what you see matches what screen readers say.
  • Changing one token and clicking through every page is the fastest consistency test there is.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a fourth page in a projects/ folder and get every path right with ../.
  • Add a "night" theme by redefining the color tokens inside @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark), then check every pair for contrast.
  • Add a small .badge component for "Free" or "New" that uses --color-brand and --color-on-brand, and put it on two event cards.
  • Make a 404 page called 404.html with the same header, for when someone types a wrong address. GitHub Pages uses it automatically.

What you'll learn

  • Know exactly what the finished capstone site must include and what you'll hand in.
  • Choose a project idea at the right difficulty for you.
  • Plan the site with a one-sentence goal, a sitemap, a content list, phone and desktop wireframes, and a set of design tokens.

Over the last six modules you built pieces: a product grid, a landing page, a club site. The capstone puts them together into one site that you design, build, and publish at a real web address you can send to anyone. Most of the hard thinking happens before the first tag, so this lesson is all planning.

#The brief

Build a website of at least three linked pages about a topic you choose, and publish it for free on GitHub Pages.

#Your site must have

  1. Semantic structure on every page: <header>, <nav>, <main>, and <footer>, with headings in order (one <h1>, then <h2>s, and so on).
  2. One shared stylesheet that starts with design tokens (custom properties for color, type sizes, and spacing). No page has its own <style> block.
  3. Flexbox and Grid: at least one layout made with each.
  4. A responsive layout that works from 320px to 1440px wide, written mobile-first, with no sideways scrolling at any width.
  5. At least one form with a <label> for every field.
  6. Images that scale, each with useful alt text (or alt="" for decoration). Use your own photos or openly licensed ones, such as Wikimedia Commons, with credit.
  7. Keyboard access: every link, button, and field reachable with Tab, a visible focus style, and a skip link.
  8. Readable color: every text and background pair at 4.5:1 or better.
  9. Respect for motion settings: any animation or transition is turned off for prefers-reduced-motion: reduce.
  10. Working relative links on the live site, including the stylesheet and images.

#What you hand in

  • The live URL (like https://yourname.github.io/my-site/) and the GitHub repository link.
  • Your planning notes from this lesson: goal, sitemap, wireframes, and tokens.
  • A short test log (you'll make it in the last lesson).
  • A two- to three-minute presentation of the site.

#Pick an idea

Choose something you know about and care about. You'll write all the text yourself, and that's much easier on a topic you could talk about for ten minutes.

Idea Pages What makes it interesting Level
Personal portfolio Home, Projects, Contact A project card grid and a contact form. Your pages from this course can be the projects. Starter
Club, team, or band site Home, Events, Join, Gallery An events list, a photo gallery with a featured image, and a sign-up form. Starter to middle
A local shop or café (invented, or a family business with permission) Home, Menu, Visit, Order A menu laid out with Grid, an hours table, and an order or booking form. Middle
A guide to something you know well (a game, a sport, a city, a hobby) 5 or more, with a subfolder Consistent navigation across many pages, paths with ../, and long-form reading typography. Stretch
An event microsite (a science fair, a hackathon, a recital) Home, Schedule, Speakers, Register A schedule built with grid-template-areas and a dark theme from prefers-color-scheme. Stretch

💡 Tip

If you can't decide, pick the portfolio. It's the most useful one to have afterward, and it grows with you: every project you build after this course can become a new card on it.

#Ideas that cause trouble

  • Anything that needs accounts, saved data, or payments. A login page, a shopping cart that remembers items, or a working checkout all need a server and a database. HTML and CSS can show what they'd look like, but can't make them work. Design the page and say so.
  • Copying a famous site. Rebuilding a big company's homepage teaches you less than you'd think, and their layouts hide a lot of complexity. Your own small site will be better.
  • Placeholder text. "Lorem ipsum" hides problems. Real headings and paragraphs of real length show you where the layout breaks.

#Plan before you code

Work through these five steps in a notes file or on paper. Keep it; it's part of what you hand in.

#1. Write one sentence

"This site is for ______, and it helps them ______." For example: "This site is for students who might join the robotics club, and it helps them find out when we meet and sign up." Every page and every section should serve that sentence. When you're unsure whether to add something, check it against the sentence.

#2. Draw the sitemap

List every page and how they link. Keep it flat: every page should be reachable from the main navigation in one click.

#3. Write the content first

For each page, list the sections and write the actual text, at least in rough form. You'll find out quickly whether a page has enough to say. A page with one sentence on it probably belongs inside another page.

Page Sections Content to gather
Home Intro, featured projects, call to action A two-sentence intro, a photo of you or your work
Projects Card grid For each project: a title, one sentence, a screenshot, a link
Contact Form, other links Which fields you need (name, email, message)

#4. Wireframe phone first, then desktop

A wireframe is a box sketch: no colors, no fonts, just where things go. Draw the phone version first, since it forces you to decide the order of importance. Then draw how the same boxes rearrange on a wide screen.

Label each box with the layout tool you'll use: "flex, space-between" for the header, "grid, auto-fit" for the cards. Now the CSS is half planned.

#5. Choose your tokens

Decide your design system before you build, and write it down:

  • Colors: text, muted text, background, surface, brand, and the text color that goes on the brand. Check every pair in the WebAIM contrast checker and write the ratio next to it.
  • Type: a body size of 1rem and a scale ratio (1.2 for calm, 1.25 for balanced, 1.333 for dramatic), giving four or five steps.
  • Spacing: five or six steps, such as 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, and 3rem.
  • Fonts: system-ui is a safe default. If you want a web font, choose one and stick with it for the whole site.

#A planning template

Copy this into a file called planning.md in your project folder and fill it in.

#A suggested schedule

Session Goal
1 Finish this plan: goal, sitemap, content, wireframes, tokens
2 Milestones 1 and 2: every page's HTML, then tokens and base styles
3 Milestones 3 and 4: layouts with Flexbox and Grid, then responsive rules
4 Milestones 5 and 6: accessibility pass, then publish on GitHub Pages
5 Test, polish, and rehearse your presentation

The next lesson gives you a starter skeleton and walks through each milestone.

#Further reading

  • web.dev: Learn Design (opens in a new tab): a free course from Google on responsive design, from layout and typography to theming. A good place to look up any design question that comes up while planning.
  • WebAIM Contrast Checker (opens in a new tab): check every color pair for your token list before you write a line of CSS.

What you'll learn
