  • Build in six milestones, checking each one before moving on.
  • Publish the site with GitHub Pages and fix the problems that usually appear on the first upload.

The fastest way to get stuck on a website is to write all the HTML, all the CSS, and all the responsive rules at once, then try to figure out which part is broken. Instead, build in milestones. Each one ends with something that works and a quick check that proves it.

#The starter skeleton

Make a project folder with this structure. Use your own page names from your plan.

Every page starts as a copy of this file. Change the <title>, move aria-current="page" to the right link, and fill in <main>.

And the stylesheet. Replace the token values with the ones from your plan; everything else already reads from them.

Here's what the skeleton looks like before you add anything:

The reduced-motion rule in section 5 is a safety net: if you add an animation later and forget about motion settings, it's switched off anyway for people who asked. You can still write gentler, specific rules of your own.

#The six milestones

# Milestone You're done when
1 Structure. Every page's real content in semantic HTML, no new CSS. Every page has one <h1>, headings go in order, every nav link opens the right page, and every image has alt.
2 Tokens and base. Your colors, type scale, and spacing in :root. You squint at each page and can tell headings from body text, and every color pair in your plan passes 4.5:1.
3 Layout. Components and layouts with Flexbox and Grid. At a laptop width, the page matches your desktop wireframe.
4 Responsive. Mobile-first rules and media queries where needed. In the device toolbar at 320, 375, 768, 1024, and 1440px, nothing scrolls sideways or overlaps.
5 Accessibility pass. Skip link, focus, contrast, labels, motion. You can use every page with only the keyboard, and the focus ring is visible on every stop.
6 Publish. The site online with GitHub Pages. The live URL works on your own phone, styles and images included.

#Milestone 1: Structure

Write each page's HTML with its real text from your plan. Resist the urge to style. A good test: with only the skeleton CSS, the page should still read well from top to bottom, because the order of the HTML is the order a screen reader and a phone will use.

Paste each page into the W3C Markup Validator (opens in a new tab) (the Validate by Direct Input tab) and fix whatever it reports, such as unclosed tags or duplicate ids.

#Milestone 2: Tokens and base

Fill in your token values. Look at each page and adjust: if headings feel too close in size to the body text, try a bigger scale ratio. Change values only in :root.

#Milestone 3: Layout

Build your components in section 6 of the stylesheet: cards, a card grid, a hero, a form layout. Most capstone sites need just three patterns: a flex row for the header (already in the skeleton), an auto-fit grid for repeated items, and maybe a two-column section. Build at a laptop width first, and don't worry about phones yet.

#Milestone 4: Responsive

Now shrink the window. Turn on the device toolbar and start at 320px. Fix the first thing that breaks, then widen until the next thing breaks. That point is where a media query belongs, whatever device it matches. Common fixes: swap a fixed width for min(), add flex-wrap: wrap, or move a two-column rule into a min-width query.

#Milestone 5: Accessibility pass

Unplug your mouse, or just don't touch it. Starting from the address bar, press Tab through every page. Check that the skip link appears first, every interactive thing is reachable, the order makes sense, and you can always see where focus is. Then re-check the contrast of anything you added after Milestone 2, and confirm every form field has a <label>.

#Milestone 6: Publish

The next section walks through it. Publishing earlier is fine too, so you can check the site on a real phone while you work. Each upload replaces the old files.

#Publishing on GitHub Pages

GitHub Pages hosts plain HTML and CSS sites for free. You need a GitHub account, and GitHub's terms require you to be 13 or older to have one. If you're younger, ask a teacher or parent to publish it from their account, or present your site from your own computer with Live Server.

  1. Sign in at github.com (opens in a new tab). In the upper-right corner, click + and choose New repository.
  2. Name it in lowercase with dashes, like my-site. Leave it Public (free accounts need a public repository for Pages). Turn on the option to add a README so the repository isn't empty, then click Create repository.
  3. On the repository's main page, open the Add file menu and choose Upload files. Open your project folder on your computer, select everything inside it (your HTML files and the css and images folders), and drag it onto the page. Don't drag the outer my-site folder itself, or your index.html will end up one level too deep.
  4. Type a short message like First upload in the commit message box. Leave the option to commit directly to the main branch selected, and click the green commit button.
  5. Click Settings at the top of the repository, then Pages in the left sidebar. Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch. In the branch menu choose main, leave the folder as / (root), and click Save.
  6. Wait a minute or two, then refresh the Pages settings page. When the site is ready, the page shows its address and a Visit site button. It can take up to 10 minutes the first time.

Your address will be https://your-username.github.io/my-site/. Open it on your phone. To update the site later, upload the changed files the same way; files with the same name replace the old ones.

#When the live site doesn't look right

What you see Likely cause Fix
A GitHub 404 page at your address index.html isn't at the top level, or it's named Index.html Make sure index.html (all lowercase) sits next to the css folder in the repository, not inside another folder
The page loads as plain black text The stylesheet path is wrong online Check the capitalization of css/styles.css exactly, and remove any leading / from the href
Some images are broken A capitalization mismatch, often .JPG versus .jpg Rename the file or fix the src so they match letter for letter
A page works locally but 404s online The link uses different capitals than the file name, or the file wasn't uploaded Compare the link and the file name in the repository
Your changes don't show up Pages hasn't rebuilt yet, or the browser cached the old file Wait a few minutes, then reload with Ctrl+Shift+R (Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac)

⚠️ Watch out

Live Server hides path mistakes. On Windows and macOS, Live Server will happily load Styles.css when you asked for styles.css. GitHub Pages won't. If something works on your laptop and breaks online, capitalization is the first suspect.

#Further reading

  • GitHub Docs: Creating a GitHub Pages site (opens in a new tab): the official steps, including how to make a user site at username.github.io without the project name in the address.
  • W3C Markup Validator (opens in a new tab): paste your HTML or enter your live URL to find unclosed tags, duplicate ids, and other structural mistakes.

m8-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Run a test plan on your live site and record the results in a test log.
  • Write up one bug: what you saw, why it happened, and how you fixed it.
  • Polish the details that visitors notice, and present the site in two to three minutes.
  • Grade your own work against the rubric before anyone else does.

Your site looks right on your laptop. That's a good start, and it's also the one setup you've been testing on all along. The real test is a stranger on a small phone with a cracked screen, a keyboard user who never touches a mouse, and someone who has turned their text size way up. This lesson checks the site for each of them.

#Step 1: Run the test plan

Do every test on the live GitHub Pages site, not on Live Server, since some bugs only appear online. Record each result in a test log like the one below, and keep it in planning.md.

# Test How Pass when
1 Five widths Device toolbar at 320, 375, 768, 1024, and 1440px, on every page No sideways scrolling, nothing overlaps or gets cut off
2 A real phone Open the live URL on your phone (or a friend's) Text is readable without zooming, and buttons are easy to tap
3 Keyboard only Tab and Shift+Tab through each page; Enter on links and buttons The skip link shows first, every control is reachable in a sensible order, and focus is always visible
4 200% zoom Ctrl or Cmd with + until the zoom reads 200% Nothing is cut off, and the page reflows instead of scrolling sideways
5 Contrast Every text and background pair in the WebAIM checker Every pair is 4.5:1 or better (3:1 for large text and focus rings)
6 Lighthouse DevTools, Lighthouse panel, Accessibility checked, Analyze page load You fixed every failed audit, or wrote down why one doesn't apply
7 Valid HTML The W3C Markup Validator (opens in a new tab), Validate by URI, with each page's live URL No errors
8 Every link Click every link on every page of the live site No 404s; every page loads with its styles and images
9 Reduced motion DevTools Command Menu, Show Rendering, emulate prefers-reduced-motion: reduce Nothing slides, spins, or smooth-scrolls
10 Form Click each label; Tab to each field; try to submit with a required field empty Clicking a label puts the cursor in its field, and the browser blocks the empty submission

Here is what one row of a filled-in log might look like:

Don't stop at the first failure. Run every test, list everything, then fix the problems one at a time, retesting after each fix.

⚠️ Watch out

A perfect Lighthouse score doesn't mean the site is accessible. Lighthouse can find missing alt attributes, missing labels, and low contrast. It can't tell whether your alt text actually describes the image, whether the focus order makes sense, or whether a heading says what the section is about. That's why tests 3 and 4 are done by a person.

#Step 2: Write up one bug

Pick the most interesting problem your tests found and write a short note about it. Four parts:

  1. What I saw: "On my phone, the contact form's Send button disappeared off the right edge."
  2. Why it happened: "The input had width: 400px, and the phone was only 375px wide, so the row was wider than the screen."
  3. How I fixed it: "I replaced the fixed width with flex: 1 1 14rem and added flex-wrap: wrap, so the button drops under the input on narrow screens."
  4. How I checked: "Retested at 320 and 375px in the device toolbar and on my phone."

This note is part of the grade, and it's also the most useful thing you can say in an interview someday. Explaining a bug clearly shows you understand the code, not just that you typed it.

#Step 3: Polish what people notice

  • Unique page titles. Each <title> should name the page and the site, like Projects | Maya Chen. It's what shows in the browser tab and in search results.
  • A short description. Add <meta name="description" content="..."> to each page's <head> with one sentence about that page. Search engines often show it under your link.
  • Consistent edges. Check that the header, the main content, and the footer line up on the left at every width. If one doesn't, it probably isn't inside a .wrap.
  • Image credits. Any photo you didn't take gets a credit in a caption or the footer, with the license name.
  • No leftovers. Delete commented-out code, test text, and unused CSS rules.
  • A 404 page. Add a 404.html with your normal header and a link home. GitHub Pages shows it automatically whenever someone visits an address that doesn't exist on your site.

#Step 4: Present it in two to three minutes

Plan your talk around the site, not around the code. A good order:

  1. The goal sentence (15 seconds): who the site is for and what it helps them do.
  2. A tour at phone width (45 seconds): show the main pages in the device toolbar or on a real phone.
  3. The same page at desktop width (20 seconds): point out what rearranged and which CSS did it.
  4. A keyboard run (20 seconds): Tab from the top, show the skip link and the focus ring.
  5. One piece of CSS you're proud of (20 seconds): your tokens, a grid, or a tricky fix.
  6. Your bug story (20 seconds) and what you'd add next (10 seconds).

Rehearse once with a timer. If you're over three minutes, cut the tour, not the bug story.

#The rubric

Each row is scored from 1 to 4, for a total of 36 points.

Criterion 4: Excellent 3: Good 2: Developing 1: Beginning
Structure Every page uses header, nav, main, footer; headings in order; validator shows no errors Landmarks on every page, one or two heading or validator issues Some pages missing landmarks, or headings chosen for size Mostly divs; headings out of order
Shared styles One stylesheet built from tokens; no page has its own styles; changing a token updates the site One stylesheet with tokens, a few raw values repeated Tokens exist but many values are hard-coded Styles copied into each page
Layout Flexbox and Grid each used where they fit best, with gap and no layout hacks Both used, with one awkward spot Only one of the two used Layout relies on fixed widths or spacing tricks
Responsive Mobile-first, works from 320 to 1440px with no sideways scroll, images scale Works at all five test widths with a minor issue Breaks at one width Breaks on phones
Accessibility Skip link, visible focus everywhere, all pairs 4.5:1, labels on every field, motion respected, keyboard test passes One small gap in the list Several gaps, but the keyboard can reach everything Keyboard users get stuck, or focus is invisible
Content and hierarchy Real, well-written content; clear hierarchy that passes the squint test; consistent spacing Clear hierarchy, a few spacing inconsistencies Hierarchy is unclear on some pages Placeholder text or no visible hierarchy
Published and linked Live URL works; every link, image, and stylesheet loads online; 404 page exists Live, with one broken link or image Live, but styles or several images missing Not published
Planning and testing Goal, sitemap, wireframes, tokens, full test log, and a clear bug write-up All parts present, one thin Plan or test log missing parts Little or no planning or testing shown
Presentation Two to three minutes, shows phone and desktop, a keyboard run, and the bug story Covers most parts, a little long or short Mostly reads code aloud Not presented

Score yourself honestly before you hand it in. Anything you rate 2 or below is your to-do list for the remaining time.

#Reflect

Write two or three sentences for each question in planning.md. These are for you, so be honest.

  • What part of the site took longer than you planned, and why?
  • Which bug taught you the most?
  • If you started over tomorrow, what would you plan differently?
  • What's one thing on a real website you now notice that you didn't before this course?

#Where to go next

You can now build sites that work for everyone on every screen. Here's where to take it:

  • Add JavaScript. It's the language that makes pages respond: menus that open, forms that check themselves, data that loads. Your HTML and CSS are the foundation it builds on.
  • Keep practicing layouts. Frontend Mentor (opens in a new tab) gives you real designs to rebuild, with free challenges at every level. Kevin Powell's free course Conquering Responsive Layouts (opens in a new tab) goes deeper on everything from Modules 5 and 6.
  • Look things up in the best references. MDN's Learn web development (opens in a new tab) and web.dev's Learn CSS (opens in a new tab) are free, accurate, and kept up to date.
  • Keep your site alive. Add every new project to it. A portfolio that grows over a year says more than any single project.
